content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 1: Short title, application and commencement

Q: What types of proceedings does the Indian law of evidence apply to?
A: It applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, including Courts-martial, but it does not apply to affidavits presented to any Court or officer, nor to proceedings before an arbitrator. [Source: Section 1, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: How does Indian evidence law define 'conclusive proof'?
A: Under clause (b), 'conclusive proof' means that when one fact is declared by the Act to be conclusive proof of another, the Court shall, on proof of the one fact, regard the other as proved, and shall not allow evidence to be given for the purpose of disproving it. [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What does Section 2 of BSA 2023 define as 'evidence'?
A: Section 2 of BSA 2023 defines 'evidence' under clause (e) to include all statements, including electronic ones, permitted or required to be made before the Court by witnesses (called oral evidence), and all documents, including electronic or digital records, produced for the Court's inspection (called documentary evidence). [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: If a person claims that a website or a voice mail message stored on a digital device is a document, is this legally correct?
A: Yes, under clause (d), an electronic record on emails, server logs, documents on computers, laptops or smartphones, messages, websites, locational evidence, and voice mail messages stored on digital devices are all explicitly considered documents. [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What are the two specific types of 'evidence' explicitly recognized under the definitions of this Act?
A: Under clause (e), the Act explicitly recognizes 'oral evidence,' which includes statements made by witnesses before the Court, and 'documentary evidence,' which includes all documents produced for the inspection of the Court. [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: When the Act directs that a Court 'shall presume' a fact, what limitation exists on this presumption?
A: Under clause (l), when a Court 'shall presume' a fact, it must regard such fact as proved, unless and until it is disproved. [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is the consequence when a fact is considered 'disproved' under the Act?
A: Under clause (c), a fact is 'disproved' when, after considering the matters before it, the Court either believes it does not exist or considers its non-existence so probable that a prudent man would act on the supposition that it does not exist. [Source: Section 2, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 3: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

Q: According to Indian law, what facts are allowed to be given in evidence during a suit or proceeding?
A: Evidence may be given in any suit or proceeding of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are declared to be relevant by the Act, and of no others. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 3: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

Q: What rule does Section 3 of BSA 2023 lay down regarding the admissibility of evidence?
A: Section 3 of BSA 2023 limits the giving of evidence strictly to the existence or non-existence of facts in issue and other facts specifically declared to be relevant, prohibiting the presentation of evidence for any other facts. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 3: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

Q: If a person is being tried for the murder of someone by beating them with a club, what kinds of facts would be considered in issue?
A: As per the illustration, facts in issue would include the person beating the victim with the club, the person causing the victim's death by such beating, and the person's intention to cause the death. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 3: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

Q: Does this section permit a person to give evidence of a fact if another civil procedure law disentitles them from doing so?
A: No, the Explanation states that this section shall not enable any person to give evidence of a fact which he is disentitled to prove by any provision of the law relating to civil procedure. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 3: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts

A: No, as shown in the illustration, they cannot produce the bond or prove its contents at a subsequent stage otherwise than in accordance with the conditions prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

Q: If a party attempts to introduce evidence of a fact that is neither in issue nor explicitly declared relevant, what is the legal outcome?
A: The evidence will not be permitted, as the Act explicitly states that evidence may be given only of facts in issue and relevant facts, and of no others. [Source: Section 3, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 4: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

Q: Can facts that are not directly in issue be considered relevant if they are closely connected to the event?
A: Yes, facts which are not in issue but are so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact as to form part of the same transaction are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 4: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

Q: What does Section 4 of BSA 2023 state about facts forming part of the same transaction?
A: Section 4 of BSA 2023 states that facts forming part of the same transaction as a fact in issue or a relevant fact are relevant, even if they occurred at different times and places. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 4: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

Q: During a beating that leads to a murder charge, if bystanders made statements during or shortly after the event, are those statements relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, whatever was said or done by the accused, the victim, or the bystanders at the beating, or so shortly before or after it as to form part of the transaction, is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 4: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

Q: What is the key requirement for a fact not directly in issue to be deemed relevant under this rule?
A: The requirement is that the fact must be so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact that it forms part of the same transaction. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 4: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction

Q: Is it necessary that the connected facts forming part of the same transaction must have occurred simultaneously at the exact same location?
A: No, the rule explicitly provides that they are relevant whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

Q: If goods are delivered to several intermediate persons successively, what is the consequence for proving the final delivery?
A: Each intermediate delivery is a relevant fact when the question is whether the goods were ultimately delivered to the final recipient. [Source: Section 4, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 5: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts

Q: Are the direct causes and effects of a relevant fact admissible in court?
A: Yes, facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts or facts in issue, or which constitute the state of things under which they happened, or which afforded an opportunity for their occurrence, are relevant. [Source: Section 5, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts

Q: How does Section 5 of BSA 2023 treat facts that provide an opportunity for an event to occur?
A: Section 5 of BSA 2023 treats facts which afforded an opportunity for the occurrence or transaction of relevant facts or facts in issue as relevant facts. [Source: Section 5, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 5: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts

Q: If a person is accused of murder, would marks on the ground from a struggle near the crime scene be relevant?
A: Yes, the illustration states that marks on the ground, produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed, are relevant facts. [Source: Section 5, BSA 2023]

Q: What categories of connected facts does this rule specifically make relevant?
A: It makes relevant the facts that are the occasion, cause, or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts, those that constitute the state of things under which they happened, and those that afforded an opportunity for their occurrence. [Source: Section 5, BSA 2023]

Q: How would a victim's known habits before being poisoned be evaluated under this rule?

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 6: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

Q: Is a person's conduct after an offence relevant in a legal proceeding?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the conduct of any party or their agent, or the conduct of any person against whom an offence is the subject of the proceeding, is relevant if such conduct influences or is influenced by a fact in issue or relevant fact, whether it was previous or subsequent to the event. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 6: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

Q: What does Section 6 of BSA 2023 establish regarding motive and preparation?
A: Section 6 of BSA 2023 establishes under sub-section (1) that any fact is relevant which shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for any fact in issue or relevant fact. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 6: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

Q: If a person accused of a crime runs away immediately after hearing someone say the police are coming for them, is their running away relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the fact that the accused ran away immediately after hearing that the police were coming is relevant as subsequent conduct. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 6: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

Q: Under what condition does a statement count as 'conduct' under this section?
A: Explanation 1 clarifies that the word 'conduct' does not include statements, unless those statements accompany and explain acts other than statements. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 6: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct

Q: Are statements made to a person completely irrelevant if they don't accompany physical acts?
A: No, Explanation 2 states that when the conduct of any person is relevant, any statement made to him or in his presence and hearing, which affects such conduct, is also relevant. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

Q: If an accused attempts to destroy or conceal evidence after a crime, how is this treated?
A: As per the illustration, the fact that the accused destroyed or concealed evidence, or prevented the presence of witnesses, is relevant as it shows conduct affected by the crime. [Source: Section 6, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 7: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: Can background facts that merely explain or introduce the main issue be presented as evidence?
A: Yes, facts that are necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or a relevant fact are themselves relevant in so far as they are necessary for that purpose. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 7: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: What does Section 7 of BSA 2023 say about facts that establish identity?
A: Section 7 of BSA 2023 states that facts which establish the identity of anything, or of a person whose identity is relevant, are relevant in so far as they are necessary for that purpose. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 7: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: If a person suddenly leaves home around the time of a crime, but they had an urgent business matter to attend to elsewhere, is the business matter relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the fact that the person had sudden and urgent business is relevant as it tends to explain the fact that they left home suddenly. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 7: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: What specific types of contextual facts are made relevant under this provision?
A: Facts are relevant if they explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, support or rebut an inference suggested by them, establish identity, fix time or place, or show the relation of parties involved in the transaction. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: If a person had urgent business when they left home, are all the intricate details of that business relevant?
A: No, the illustration clarifies that the details of the business are not relevant, except in so far as they are necessary to show that the business was sudden and urgent. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts

Q: How does the law treat the cries of a mob when trying a person for participating in a riot?
A: The illustration shows that the cries of the mob are relevant as explanatory of the nature of the transaction. [Source: Section 7, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: When people plot together to commit a crime, can the actions of one conspirator be used as evidence against the others?
A: Yes, where there is reasonable ground to believe two or more persons conspired, anything said, done, or written by any of them in reference to their common intention is a relevant fact against each person believed to be conspiring. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: What rule does Section 8 of BSA 2023 establish regarding conspiracies?
A: Section 8 of BSA 2023 establishes that once a reasonable ground exists to believe a conspiracy exists, actions or statements by any conspirator regarding their common intention are relevant against all conspirators. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: If someone joins a conspiracy later, are the actions taken by other conspirators before they joined relevant against them?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, acts by other conspirators are relevant against a person even if they took place before he joined the conspiracy or after he left it, and even if he was ignorant of them. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: What is the threshold requirement before a conspirator's statement can be used against another under this section?
A: There must be a reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together to commit an offence or an actionable wrong. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: Are statements made by a conspirator relevant if they were made before the common intention was formed?
A: No, the section specifies that the things said, done, or written must occur after the time when such intention was first entertained by any one of them. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 8: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design

Q: For what specific legal purposes can the actions of one conspirator be used in court?
A: The actions can be used both for the purpose of proving the existence of the conspiracy itself and for the purpose of showing that any specific person was a party to it. [Source: Section 8, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 9: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

Q: Can a fact that has no direct connection to a case become legally relevant if it makes another important fact highly improbable?
A: Yes, facts not otherwise relevant become relevant if by themselves or in connection with other facts they make the existence or non-existence of any fact in issue or relevant fact highly probable or improbable. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 9: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

Q: What does Section 9 of BSA 2023 say about facts that are inconsistent with a fact in issue?
A: Section 9 of BSA 2023 states under clause (1) that facts not otherwise relevant become relevant if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 9: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

Q: If a person is accused of committing a crime in Chennai on a certain day, but they can prove they were in Ladakh on that day, is this fact relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the fact that the accused was in Ladakh is relevant because it is inconsistent with the fact in issue of them committing a crime in Chennai on the same day. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 9: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant

Q: Under what two conditions does this section make an otherwise irrelevant fact relevant?
A: The fact becomes relevant if it is either inconsistent with a fact in issue or relevant fact, or if it makes the existence or non-existence of such a fact highly probable or improbable. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

Q: If it is only 'highly improbable' rather than completely 'impossible' for someone to have committed a crime due to their distance from the scene, is that distance still relevant?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that even if the distance renders their involvement highly improbable, though not impossible, the fact is still relevant. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

Q: If circumstances show a crime must have been committed by A, B, C, or D, what happens if evidence shows B, C, and D did not commit it?
A: The illustration shows that every fact which proves the crime could have been committed by no one else, and that B, C, or D did not commit it, is relevant to proving A committed it. [Source: Section 9, BSA 2023]

Q: In cases where a party is seeking monetary compensation, what kinds of facts can be introduced to help calculate the payout?
A: In suits where damages are claimed, any fact which will enable the Court to determine the amount of damages which ought to be awarded is relevant. [Source: Section 10, BSA 2023]

A: Section 10 of BSA 2023 lays down that in suits in which damages are claimed, any fact enabling the Court to determine the amount of damages to be awarded is relevant. [Source: Section 10, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 11: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

Q: When the existence of a right or custom is disputed, what kind of evidence is relevant?
A: Any transaction by which the right or custom was created, claimed, modified, recognised, asserted, or denied, or which was inconsistent with its existence, and particular instances where it was claimed, recognised, or exercised, are relevant facts. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

Q: What does Section 11 of BSA 2023 state about proving rights or customs?
A: Section 11 of BSA 2023 states that where the question is as to the existence of any right or custom, transactions creating, modifying, or denying it, and particular instances of its exercise or dispute, are relevant facts. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 11: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

Q: If A claims a right to a fishery, would a past mortgage of that fishery by A's father be relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, a mortgage of the fishery by A's father, along with deeds conferring it or instances where neighbors stopped its exercise, are relevant facts. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 11: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

Q: What two specific categories of facts are made relevant when a right or custom is in question?
A: The two categories are: (a) any transaction affecting the creation, claim, or denial of the right or custom, and (b) particular instances in which its exercise was claimed, disputed, or departed from. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 11: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

Q: Is evidence limited only to transactions that explicitly assert or confirm the right or custom?
A: No, under clause (a), the section explicitly includes transactions that denied the right or custom, or which were inconsistent with its existence. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 11: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

Q: What legal weight is given to particular historical instances where the exercise of a right was disputed or stopped by others?
A: Such instances are legally relevant facts that can be introduced as evidence when determining whether the right actually exists. [Source: Section 11, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: How can someone's intention, good faith, or ill-will be proven in court?
A: Facts showing the existence of any state of mind, such as intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, or ill-will towards a particular person, are relevant when the existence of that state of mind is in issue or relevant. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: What does Section 12 of BSA 2023 say about proving physical or bodily conditions?
A: Section 12 of BSA 2023 states that facts showing the existence of any state of body or bodily feeling are relevant when the existence of such state of body or bodily feeling is in issue or relevant. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: If a person sues an owner for damage done by a ferocious dog, can the plaintiff introduce evidence that the dog had previously bitten others?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that the fact that the dog had previously bitten X, Y, and Z, and that they had made complaints to the owner, are relevant facts to show the owner's knowledge. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: What specific limitation does Explanation 1 place on proving a state of mind?
A: Explanation 1 clarifies that a fact relevant as showing the existence of a relevant state of mind must show that the state of mind exists, not generally, but in reference to the particular matter in question. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: If an accused has previously committed a relevant offence to show their state of mind, is their formal conviction for that past offence admissible?
A: Yes, Explanation 2 states that where the previous commission of an offence is relevant, the previous conviction of such person shall also be a relevant fact. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 12: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

Q: If a person makes statements about their symptoms while suffering an illness, and their cause of death is later questioned, what happens to those statements?
A: According to the illustration, statements made by the person during their illness as to their symptoms are treated as relevant facts. [Source: Section 12, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: How can the law distinguish whether an act was merely accidental or done intentionally?
A: When there is a question whether an act was accidental or intentional, the fact that such act formed part of a series of similar occurrences, in each of which the person doing the act was concerned, is relevant. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: What does Section 13 of BSA 2023 establish regarding a series of similar occurrences?
A: Section 13 of BSA 2023 establishes that if an act forms part of a series of similar occurrences involving the same person, this is relevant to determining whether the act was accidental or intentional. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: If a person's house burns down and they claim insurance, can the fact that several of their previous houses also burned down and resulted in insurance payouts be used as evidence?
A: Yes, the illustration explains that these facts are relevant as they form a series of similar occurrences, tending to show that the fires were not accidental. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: What are the necessary conditions for a past occurrence to be relevant in showing an act was not accidental?
A: The act must form part of a series of similar occurrences, and in each of those occurrences, the person doing the act must have been concerned. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: Does this section apply if the person doing the act was completely unconnected to the other similar occurrences?
A: No, the section specifically requires that the person doing the act was 'concerned' in each occurrence within the series. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 13: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

Q: If an employee makes a false entry in a ledger under-reporting what they received, how does finding other false entries in their favor affect the case?
A: As per the illustration, the fact that other entries made by the employee are false and in their favor is relevant to prove the false entry was intentional rather than accidental. [Source: Section 13, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: Can established business routines be used as evidence to prove an act happened?
A: Yes, when there is a question whether a particular act was done, the existence of any course of business, according to which it naturally would have been done, is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: What principle is codified in Section 14 of BSA 2023?
A: Section 14 of BSA 2023 codifies that the existence of any course of business, according to which an act would naturally have been done, is relevant to determining if the act was actually done. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: If there is a dispute over whether a specific letter was dispatched, is evidence of the office's general mailing routine relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the fact that it was the ordinary course of business for all letters put in a certain place to be carried to the post is relevant. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: What element must be shown for a course of business to be relevant?
A: It must be shown that an established course of business existed, according to which the particular act in question naturally would have been done. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: Is it necessary to definitively prove the specific execution of the act if the general course of business is shown?
A: The section makes the existence of the course of business itself a relevant fact to infer the act was done, even without direct proof of the specific execution. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 14: Existence of course of business when relevant

Q: How can one prove that a letter reached its intended recipient using this section?
A: The illustration shows that proving the letter was posted in due course and was not returned through the Return Letter Office makes it relevant to conclude it reached the recipient. [Source: Section 14, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Existence of course of business when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: How is a legal admission defined in the context of evidence?
A: An admission is a statement, whether oral, documentary, or contained in electronic form, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and which is made by specific persons under specific circumstances. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: What does Section 15 of BSA 2023 cover?
A: Section 15 of BSA 2023 defines an 'admission' as a statement in oral, documentary, or electronic form that suggests an inference regarding a fact in issue or a relevant fact. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: If a person sends a WhatsApp message that indirectly hints at their liability in a case, can this be considered an admission?
A: Yes, because an admission includes statements contained in 'electronic form' which suggest any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: What are the core components that make a statement an admission under this section?
A: The statement must be oral, documentary, or electronic; it must suggest an inference regarding a fact in issue or relevant fact; and it must be made by the persons and under the circumstances mentioned in subsequent sections. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: Is a statement an admission if it is completely unrelated to the facts in issue or relevant facts?
A: No, the definition explicitly requires that the statement must suggest an inference as to a fact in issue or a relevant fact. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 15: Admission defined

Q: What is the legal effect of classifying an electronic statement as an admission under this section?
A: The consequence is that the electronic statement is legally treated as an admission and may be introduced into evidence, subject to the rules governing who made it and under what circumstances. [Source: Section 15, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission defined

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: Are statements made by someone acting on behalf of a party considered admissions?
A: Yes, statements made by an agent to any party, whom the Court regards as expressly or impliedly authorised by the party to make them, are considered admissions. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: What does Section 16 of BSA 2023 establish regarding admissions by parties in a representative character?
A: Section 16 of BSA 2023 establishes that statements made by parties to suits suing or sued in a representative character are not admissions unless they were made while the party making them actually held that character. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: If a person previously owned a piece of land and made a statement about its boundaries before selling it, is that statement considered an admission against the current owner?
A: Yes, statements made by persons from whom the parties to the suit have derived their interest in the subject matter are admissions, provided they were made during the continuance of the interest of the persons making them. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: What are the conditions for a statement by a person with a proprietary or pecuniary interest to be an admission?
A: The person must have a proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject matter of the proceeding, and the statement must be made in their character of persons so interested, during the continuance of their interest. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: If a guardian of a minor makes a statement before they were officially appointed as guardian, is it an admission in a suit involving the minor?
A: No, because statements by parties suing or sued in a representative character are not admissions unless made while the party actually held that representative character. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 16: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

Q: What is the legal effect when a Court determines an agent was impliedly authorized to make a statement?
A: The consequence is that the agent's statement is legally treated as an admission against the party to the proceeding. [Source: Section 16, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admission by party to proceeding or his agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: Can statements by a third party be considered admissions against a party to a suit?
A: Yes, statements made by persons whose position or liability it is necessary to prove against a party to the suit are admissions, if such statements would be relevant against those persons in a suit brought by or against them. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: What does Section 17 of BSA 2023 cover regarding statements by third parties?
A: Section 17 of BSA 2023 covers admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against a party to the suit, making their statements admissions if they would be relevant against them in their own suit. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: A undertakes to collect rent for B, but B sues A for not collecting rent from C. If C states that he owed rent to B, is C's statement an admission?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, C's statement that he owed B rent is an admission and is relevant against A, if A denies that C owed rent to B. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: What are the specific requirements for a third party's statement to be an admission under this section?
A: The person's position or liability must be necessary to prove against a party to the suit, the statement must be relevant against the person making it in a suit involving them, and it must be made whilst they occupy that position or are subject to that liability. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: Would the third party's statement be an admission if it were made after they no longer occupied the relevant position or were no longer subject to the liability?
A: No, the section explicitly requires that the statements must be made whilst the person making them occupies such position or is subject to such liability. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 17: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

Q: How does a relevant statement by a third party whose liability must be proved affect the main party in the suit?
A: The statement functions legally as an admission, allowing it to be used as evidence against the main party in the suit to establish that specific position or liability. [Source: Section 17, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons whose position must be proved as against party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: If a party to a dispute tells the other party to ask a specific person for information, is that person's response binding as an admission?
A: Yes, statements made by persons to whom a party to the suit has expressly referred for information in reference to a matter in dispute are legally considered admissions. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: What does Section 18 of BSA 2023 state about referring to another person for information?
A: Section 18 of BSA 2023 states that if a party to a suit expressly refers someone to another person for information regarding a disputed matter, statements made by that referred person are considered admissions. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: A sells a horse to B. B questions its soundness, and A says, 'Go and ask C, C knows all about it.' Is C's statement about the horse an admission against A?
A: Yes, as per the illustration, because A expressly referred B to C for information regarding the disputed matter, C's subsequent statement is an admission. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: What condition must be met for a statement by an outside person to be an admission under this section?
A: The party to the suit must have expressly referred to that outside person for information in reference to a matter in dispute. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: Does this section apply if the party casually mentioned the person without expressly referring them for information on the dispute?
A: No, the rule requires that the party must have expressly referred to the person for information specifically in reference to the matter in dispute. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 18: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

Q: What legal standing does the statement of the referred person acquire under this rule?
A: The statement made by the referred person acquires the legal standing of an admission against the party who made the referral. [Source: Section 18, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions by persons expressly referred to by party to suit

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: Can a person use their own admission as evidence in their favor during a trial?
A: Generally, admissions cannot be proved by or on behalf of the person who makes them, except in three specific cases, such as when the statement is of a state of mind accompanied by conduct, or would be relevant between third persons if the maker were dead. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: What general rule does Section 19 of BSA 2023 establish regarding who can prove an admission?
A: Section 19 of BSA 2023 establishes that admissions are relevant and may be proved as against the person who makes them, but generally cannot be proved by or on behalf of the person who makes them. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: If a ship captain is accused of intentionally taking his ship off course, can he produce his own logbook as evidence that he stayed on course?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the captain may prove the statements in his logbook because they would be admissible between third parties if he were dead, falling under an exception in this section. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: What are the three exceptions under which a person can prove their own admission?
A: A person can prove their own admission if: (1) it would be relevant between third persons if the maker were dead; (2) it states a relevant state of mind or body accompanied by conduct rendering falsehood improbable; or (3) it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: Under what circumstance can a person accused of receiving stolen goods use their own statement of refusing to sell them below value as evidence?
A: They may prove these statements because they are explanatory of conduct influenced by facts in issue, fitting the exception where an admission is relevant otherwise than as an admission. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 19: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

Q: If A and B dispute whether a deed is forged, and A affirms it is genuine while B claims it is forged, who can prove whose statements?
A: The illustration clarifies that A may prove a statement by B that the deed is genuine, and B may prove a statement by A that the deed is forged; however, neither can prove their own statements in their favor. [Source: Section 19, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: Are oral admissions regarding the contents of a written document generally admissible in court?
A: No, oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant unless the party proposing to prove them shows they are entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents, or unless the genuineness of the produced document is in question. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: What restriction does Section 20 of BSA 2023 place on oral admissions concerning documents?
A: Section 20 of BSA 2023 restricts oral admissions as to the contents of a document from being relevant, except when secondary evidence is legally permissible or the genuineness of the document itself is disputed. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: If a party wants to introduce an oral admission about what a lost contract stated, can they do so?
A: Yes, because the contract is lost, the party would be entitled to give secondary evidence of its contents, making the oral admission about its contents relevant under this section. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: What are the two specific conditions under which an oral admission as to the contents of a document becomes relevant?
A: It becomes relevant if the party is entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of the document, or if the genuineness of a document produced in court is in question. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: Is there any situation where an oral admission about a document is relevant even if the original document is available and secondary evidence is not allowed?
A: Yes, the oral admission is relevant if the genuineness of the document produced in court is in question. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 20: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

Q: What happens if a party tries to prove an oral admission about a document's contents without meeting the required conditions?
A: The oral admission will be deemed not relevant and will not be accepted as evidence in the proceeding. [Source: Section 20, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: When oral admissions as to contents of documents are relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: Can an admission be used in a civil case if the parties agreed it shouldn't be used as evidence?
A: No, in civil cases, an admission is not relevant if it is made either upon an express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or under circumstances from which the Court can infer that the parties agreed together that evidence of it should not be given. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: What rule does Section 21 of BSA 2023 set for civil cases regarding conditional admissions?
A: Section 21 of BSA 2023 sets the rule that no admission is relevant in civil cases if it is made on the express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or if the Court infers the parties agreed not to give evidence of it. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: If two parties in a civil dispute have a settlement discussion under a strict non-disclosure agreement, can statements made during that discussion be used as admissions in court?
A: No, because the circumstances would allow the Court to infer that the parties agreed together that evidence of it should not be given, making the admission irrelevant. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: What are the two specific conditions under which an admission becomes irrelevant in a civil case?
A: The admission becomes irrelevant if it is made upon an express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or under circumstances allowing the Court to infer that the parties agreed evidence of it should not be given. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: Does an agreement to not use an admission as evidence prevent an advocate from being compelled to testify about certain matters?
A: No, the Explanation clarifies that nothing in this section exempts any advocate from giving evidence of any matter of which he may be compelled to give evidence under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 132. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 21: Admissions in civil cases when relevant

Q: What happens if a party attempts to introduce a statement made during a confidential settlement negotiation as an admission?
A: The Court will deem the admission irrelevant and exclude it from evidence, provided it infers the parties had an agreement not to give evidence of it. [Source: Section 21, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: Is a confession admissible if the accused was threatened or promised a lighter sentence by a person in authority?
A: No, a confession is irrelevant in a criminal proceeding if the making of it appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat, coercion, or promise having reference to the charge, proceeding from a person in authority. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: What does Section 22 of BSA 2023 say about confessions obtained through coercion or promises?
A: Section 22 of BSA 2023 states that a confession by an accused is irrelevant if the Court believes it was caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise from a person in authority, giving the accused reasonable grounds to suppose they would gain an advantage or avoid an evil. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: If a police officer tells a suspect, 'Confess, and I'll make sure you don't go to jail,' and the suspect confesses, can this be used in court?
A: No, this confession is irrelevant because it was caused by a promise having reference to the charge, proceeding from a person in authority, which gave the accused grounds to suppose they would avoid a temporal evil. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: What must be proven for a confession to be deemed irrelevant under the main rule of this section?
A: It must appear to have been caused by inducement, threat, coercion, or promise regarding the charge, proceeding from a person in authority, and sufficient to give the accused reasonable grounds to believe they would gain an advantage or avoid an evil of a temporal nature. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: Does a confession become irrelevant merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy or while the accused was drunk?
A: No, the second proviso states that if a confession is otherwise relevant, it does not become irrelevant merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy, in consequence of deception, when drunk, or in answer to questions they need not have answered. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 22: Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise, when irrelevant in criminal proceeding

Q: What happens if a confession is made after the impression of a previous threat or promise has been fully removed?
A: The first proviso states that if the confession is made after the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, coercion, or promise has, in the opinion of the Court, been fully removed, it becomes relevant. [Source: Section 22, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: Can a confession made directly to a police officer be used as evidence against an accused person?
A: No, no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: What strict rule does Section 23 of BSA 2023 impose regarding police confessions?
A: Section 23 of BSA 2023 imposes the rule that no confession made to a police officer, or made by any person while in police custody (unless in the immediate presence of a Magistrate), shall be proved against them. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: If a suspect in police custody confesses to a crime while a Magistrate is sitting right next to them in the room, is the confession admissible?
A: Yes, because sub-section (2) allows a confession made while in police custody to be proved against the person if it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: What are the two distinct prohibitions regarding confessions related to police under this section?
A: The section prohibits proving any confession made directly to a police officer, and it also prohibits proving any confession made by a person while in the custody of a police officer, unless a Magistrate is immediately present. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: If a person in police custody gives information that leads the police to discover a hidden murder weapon, can that specific part of the information be used?
A: Yes, the proviso states that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person in police custody, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved, whether it amounts to a confession or not. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confession to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 23: Confession to police officer

Q: If the prosecution attempts to base its entire case on a written confession the accused gave to the investigating police officer, what will the court do?
A: The court will reject the confession, as sub-section (1) strictly dictates that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved against an accused person. [Source: Section 23, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 24: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Q: If several people are tried together for the same crime, and one confesses, implicating the others, can the court use that confession against the co-accused?
A: Yes, when more persons than one are being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one affecting himself and some other of such persons is proved, the Court may take into consideration such confession as against such other person as well as against the maker. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 24: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Q: What does Section 24 of BSA 2023 state about the confessions of co-accused persons?
A: Section 24 of BSA 2023 states that if multiple persons are tried jointly for the same offence, a proved confession by one that affects both himself and a co-accused may be taken into consideration by the Court against the co-accused. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 24: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Q: A and B are jointly tried for the murder of C. If it is proved that A said, 'B and I murdered C,' how can the Court treat this statement?
A: According to the illustration, the Court may consider the effect of A's confession as against B, because they are being jointly tried for the same offence. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 24: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Q: What conditions must be met for a confession to be considered against a person other than the maker?
A: More than one person must be tried jointly for the same offence, the confession must be proved, and the confession must affect both the person making it and the other person. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 24: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Q: If an accused has absconded and is being tried in their absence alongside another present accused, does the rule of joint trial still apply?
A: Yes, Explanation II states that a trial held in the absence of an accused who has absconded or failed to comply with a proclamation under section 84 of the BNSS 2023 shall be deemed to be a joint trial for the purpose of this section. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

Q: If A is being tried alone for a murder, and the prosecution introduces a statement by B saying 'A and I murdered C,' what will the Court do?
A: As per the illustration, the statement may not be taken into consideration by the Court against A, because B is not being jointly tried with A. [Source: Section 24, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 25: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Q: If a person makes an admission, is it considered absolute and unchangeable proof of the fact admitted?
A: No, admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted, but they may operate as estoppels under the provisions of the Act. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 25: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Q: What rule does Section 25 of BSA 2023 lay down regarding the evidentiary value of admissions?
A: Section 25 of BSA 2023 lays down that admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters admitted, though they may operate as estoppels. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 25: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Q: If a person admits to owing a debt in a letter but later finds documents proving they already paid it, does their initial admission conclusively seal their fate?
A: No, because admissions are not conclusive proof, meaning the person can still introduce the newly found documents to disprove their initial admission, unless the admission operates as an estoppel. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 25: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Q: What are the two distinct legal characteristics of admissions highlighted in this section?
A: The section highlights that admissions are not conclusive proof of the matters they admit, but they possess the legal capacity to operate as estoppels. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 25: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Q: Under this specific section, is there any situation where an admission is explicitly declared to be conclusive proof?
A: No, the section explicitly states without exception that admissions are not conclusive proof, although it notes they may operate as estoppels. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

Q: If an admission operates as an estoppel in a case, what is the practical outcome for the person who made it?
A: While the admission itself isn't conclusive proof, its operation as an estoppel prevents the person from denying the truth of the admitted matter in that specific proceeding. [Source: Section 25, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 26: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

Q: Are statements made by a deceased person ever admissible as evidence in court?
A: Yes, statements of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, are themselves relevant facts in specific cases, such as when the statement relates to the cause of their death. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 26: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

Q: What rule does Section 26 of BSA 2023 provide for statements by persons whose attendance cannot be procured?
A: Section 26 of BSA 2023 provides that statements made by persons who are dead, cannot be found, or whose attendance involves unreasonable delay or expense, are relevant facts in specific circumstances. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 26: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

Q: If a person is murdered and their dying statement points to their killer, is that statement admissible even if they didn't expect to die when they made it?
A: Yes, under clause (a), statements as to the cause of death are relevant whether the person was or was not under expectation of death when they made them. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 26: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

Q: Under what circumstances does a statement made in the ordinary course of business become relevant when the maker cannot testify?
A: Under clause (b), it becomes relevant if it was made in the ordinary course of business, such as entries in account books, acknowledgements of receipt, or the date of a usually dated letter, provided the maker is dead, lost, or unavailable. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 26: Cases in which statement of relevant fact by person who is dead or cannot be found, etc., is relevant

Q: Is there any exception for admitting statements that would expose the maker to a criminal prosecution?
A: Yes, under clause (c), a statement by an unavailable person is relevant if it is against their pecuniary or proprietary interest, or if it would expose them to a criminal prosecution or a suit for damages. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

Q: How can the court establish the date of birth of a person if the attending surgeon is deceased?
A: As per the illustration, an entry in the diary of the deceased surgeon regularly kept in the course of business, stating that he attended the mother and delivered the child, is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 26, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 27: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

Q: Can evidence given by a witness in a previous trial be used in a later proceeding if the witness has died?
A: Yes, evidence given by a witness in a judicial proceeding is relevant for proving the truth of the facts it states in a subsequent judicial proceeding if the witness is dead, cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 27: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

Q: What does Section 27 of BSA 2023 stipulate regarding evidence from previous judicial proceedings?
A: Section 27 of BSA 2023 stipulates that evidence from a previous judicial proceeding can be relevant in a later proceeding to prove the truth of its facts, provided the witness is dead or otherwise unavailable, and certain conditions are met. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 27: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

Q: If an adverse party deliberately keeps a witness out of the way so they cannot testify, can that witness's past testimony be used instead?
A: Yes, the section explicitly states that if the witness is kept out of the way by the adverse party, their past evidence is relevant for proving the facts it states. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 27: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

Q: What three conditions must be satisfied to use a previous witness's testimony against a party in a subsequent proceeding?
A: The proceeding must be between the same parties or their representatives, the adverse party must have had the right and opportunity to cross-examine in the first proceeding, and the questions in issue must be substantially the same. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 27: Relevancy of certain evidence for proving, in subsequent proceeding, truth of facts therein stated

Q: Does the requirement that proceedings must be 'between the same parties' apply literally in criminal trials?
A: The Explanation clarifies that a criminal trial or inquiry shall be deemed to be a proceeding between the prosecutor and the accused within the meaning of this section. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

content:

Q: What happens if procuring a witness for a later stage of the same trial involves unreasonable delay or expense?
A: The court may consider their previously given evidence in the same judicial proceeding relevant for proving the truth of its facts. [Source: Section 27, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 28: Entries in books of account when relevant

Q: Are business account books sufficient on their own to hold someone legally liable for a debt?
A: No, entries in books of account are relevant when they refer to a matter the Court must inquire into, but such statements alone are not sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability. [Source: Section 28, BSA 2023]

Q: What rule does Section 28 of BSA 2023 establish for account books?
A: Section 28 of BSA 2023 establishes that entries in books of account regularly kept in the course of business, including electronic ones, are relevant but insufficient alone to prove liability. [Source: Section 28, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 28: Entries in books of account when relevant

Q: A sues B for one thousand rupees and presents his account book showing B's debt. Is B automatically held liable based solely on this book?
A: No, according to the illustration, while the entries are relevant, they are not sufficient without other evidence to prove the debt. [Source: Section 28, BSA 2023]

A: The entries must be in books of account, including those in electronic form, they must be regularly kept in the course of business, and they must refer to a matter the Court has to inquire into. [Source: Section 28, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 29: Relevancy of entry in public record or an electronic record made in performance of duty

Q: Is an entry made by a government official in a public register considered relevant evidence in court?
A: Yes, an entry in any public or official book, register, or electronic record stating a fact in issue or relevant fact is itself a relevant fact if made by a public servant discharging their official duty. [Source: Section 29, BSA 2023]

Q: What does Section 29 of BSA 2023 say about entries in official records?
A: Section 29 of BSA 2023 states that an entry in a public or official record, whether physical or electronic, made by a public servant or person performing a legally enjoined duty, is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 29, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of entry in public record or an electronic record made in performance of duty
