Q: If a birth is recorded in a municipal electronic register by an officer performing their statutory duty, is that entry relevant to prove the birth?
A: Yes, an entry in an electronic record made by a person in performance of a duty specially enjoined by law is itself a relevant fact. [Source: Section 29, BSA 2023]

Q: Are commercially published maps or government charts considered relevant evidence in legal disputes?
A: Yes, statements of facts made in published maps or charts generally offered for public sale, or in maps or plans made under the authority of the Government, are themselves relevant facts. [Source: Section 30, BSA 2023]

Q: If a judge needs to verify a public fact stated in a digital copy of the Official Gazette, can that digital copy be used?
A: Yes, the section explicitly includes statements in electronic or digital form purporting to be such Gazette as relevant facts. [Source: Section 31, BSA 2023]

content:

Q: What are the acceptable sources for a statement of a public fact to be considered relevant under this section?
A: The acceptable sources are recitals in any Central Act or State Act, or notifications in the Official Gazette (printed or electronic) by the Central or State Government. [Source: Section 31, BSA 2023]

content:

Q: Is a statement of a private, non-public fact relevant if it happens to be printed in the Official Gazette?
A: No, the section specifically limits relevancy to statements regarding the 'existence of any fact of a public nature.' [Source: Section 31, BSA 2023]

Q: When a Court has to form an opinion on a public fact, what evidentiary status is given to a related Central Act recital?
A: The recital is legally elevated to the status of a relevant fact, meaning it can be introduced and considered as evidence to help the Court form its opinion. [Source: Section 31, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 32: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

Q: If a court needs to determine the law of a foreign country, can it rely on a digital law book from that country?
A: Yes, any statement of such law contained in a book, including in electronic or digital form, published under the authority of that country's Government is relevant. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 32: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

Q: What does Section 32 of BSA 2023 establish regarding law books and court rulings?
A: Section 32 of BSA 2023 establishes that statements of law in government-authorized books, and reports of court rulings in published books (both including digital forms), are relevant for forming an opinion on a country's law. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 32: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

Q: A lawyer cites an electronic database purporting to contain reports of rulings from the courts of another country. Is this relevant?
A: Yes, a report of a ruling of the Courts of such country contained in a book including in electronic or digital form purporting to be a report of such rulings is relevant. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 32: Relevancy of statements as to any law contained in law books including electronic or digital form

Q: What are the two types of legal materials made relevant by this section?
A: The two types are statements of law in books published under the authority of the Government, and reports of rulings of the Courts contained in published books. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

content:

Q: Would a self-published, unauthorized blog post claiming to state a country's law be relevant under this section?
A: No, the section requires the statement of law to be contained in a book purporting to be printed or published under the authority of the Government of such country. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

Q: What is the practical effect of this rule for a judge trying to interpret foreign law?
A: The judge is legally permitted to consider government-authorized law books and published case law reports as relevant evidence to understand that foreign law. [Source: Section 32, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: When only a small part of a long conversation is relevant, does the entire conversation need to be submitted as evidence?
A: No, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the conversation as the Court considers necessary for a full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement and its circumstances. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: What principle does Section 33 of BSA 2023 establish regarding partial statements?
A: Section 33 of BSA 2023 establishes that when a statement forms part of a larger context, like a document, book, or electronic record, only as much of it as the Court considers necessary for full understanding shall be given in evidence. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: If an incriminating statement is found in one email within a chain of fifty emails, must all fifty emails be presented in court?
A: No, the Court will only require evidence of so much of the connected series of letters or papers as it considers necessary for a full understanding of the statement. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: What specific types of larger contexts does this section list as containing statements?
A: The section lists a longer statement, a conversation, an isolated document, a book, an electronic record, or a connected series of letters or papers. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: Is there a rigid rule on exactly how many sentences surrounding a statement must be included?
A: No, the limit is determined by what 'the Court considers necessary in that particular case' to fully understand the statement and the circumstances under which it was made. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 33: What evidence to be given when statement forms part of a conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers

Q: What happens if a party tries to introduce hundreds of pages of irrelevant book text just because one sentence is relevant?
A: The Court will limit the evidence to 'so much and no more' of the book as is necessary to understand the relevant statement, excluding the unnecessary portions. [Source: Section 33, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: Can an old court judgment be used as evidence to stop a new trial on the exact same matter?
A: Yes, the existence of any judgment, order, or decree which by law prevents a Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial is a relevant fact when the question is whether the Court ought to hold the trial. [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: What does Section 34 of BSA 2023 state about previous judgments?
A: Section 34 of BSA 2023 states that a previous judgment, order, or decree is a relevant fact if its existence legally prevents a Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial. [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: If a person is sued for a debt they already successfully defended in a previous lawsuit, can they present the old judgment?
A: Yes, the previous judgment is a relevant fact because it legally bars the second suit under principles like res judicata. [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: What specific condition must a prior judgment meet to be relevant under this section?
A: The prior judgment, order, or decree must be one that 'by law prevents any Court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial.' [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: Does this section make all previous judgments relevant for any purpose whatsoever?
A: No, it only makes them relevant 'when the question is whether such Court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.' [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 34: Previous judgments relevant to bar a second suit or trial

Q: When a relevant prior judgment is proven under this section, what happens to the second suit?
A: The Court uses the prior judgment as evidence to determine that it is legally barred from holding the second trial, leading to the dismissal or rejection of the new suit. [Source: Section 34, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: Are judgments from specialized courts like matrimonial or probate courts conclusive proof of the legal status they grant?
A: Yes, a final judgment of a competent Court in probate, matrimonial, admiralty, or insolvency jurisdiction which confers or takes away a legal character is conclusive proof of that character. [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: What does Section 35 of BSA 2023 dictate about judgments in probate and matrimonial jurisdictions?
A: Section 35 of BSA 2023 dictates that final judgments in these specific jurisdictions that confer or take away absolute legal character are relevant and serve as conclusive proof of that legal character. [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: If a matrimonial court issues a final decree of divorce declaring two people unmarried, can one of them later argue they are still legally married?
A: No, because sub-section (2) states that such a decree taking away a legal character is 'conclusive proof' that the legal character ceased at the time declared by the judgment. [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: Which four specific jurisdictions are covered by the strict rules of this section?
A: The four jurisdictions are probate, matrimonial, admiralty, and insolvency jurisdiction. [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: Does this section apply to a judgment that only grants a right against a specific person, rather than against the world?
A: No, the section explicitly specifies that the judgment must confer or declare entitlement to a character or thing 'not as against any specified person but absolutely.' [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 35: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

Q: What is the evidentiary weight of a probate judgment declaring property belongs to a specific person?
A: It is conclusive proof that the property belonged to that person at the time from which the judgment declared it to be his property. [Source: Section 35, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy of certain judgments in probate, etc., jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: Can a court judgment about a public matter be used as evidence in a different case about the same public matter?
A: Yes, judgments, orders, or decrees are relevant if they relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry, even if they aren't conclusive proof of what they state. [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: What does Section 36 of BSA 2023 establish about judgments relating to public matters?
A: Section 36 of BSA 2023 establishes that judgments, orders, or decrees relating to matters of a public nature are relevant to the enquiry, though they are not conclusive proof. [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: If A sues B for trespassing and B claims a public right of way, can B use a previous decree where C successfully claimed the same public right of way against A?
A: Yes, the illustration shows that the existence of the previous decree in favor of C is relevant because it relates to a matter of a public nature, but it is not conclusive proof. [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: What type of matter must a judgment relate to in order to be relevant under this section?
A: The judgment, order, or decree must relate to 'matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry.' [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: Is a judgment relevant under this section considered absolute, unquestionable proof?
A: No, the section explicitly states that 'such judgments, orders or decrees are not conclusive proof of that which they state.' [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 36: Relevancy and effect of judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in section 35

Q: When a relevant judgment about a public right of way is introduced in a new case, how must the Court treat it?
A: The Court must accept the judgment as relevant evidence to be considered, but it cannot treat it as automatically settling the question, as it is not conclusive proof. [Source: Section 36, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 37: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

Q: Are general court judgments typically relevant in unrelated cases involving different parties?
A: No, judgments, orders, or decrees other than those previously mentioned are irrelevant, unless their existence is a fact in issue or relevant under some other provision. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 37: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

Q: What general rule does Section 37 of BSA 2023 set for the relevancy of most judgments?
A: Section 37 of BSA 2023 sets the rule that most judgments, orders, or decrees are irrelevant, unless they fall under specific previous sections, are a fact in issue, or are relevant under other provisions. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 37: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

Q: If A gets a decree against C for libel, can B use that same decree to automatically win a separate libel suit against C?
A: No, according to the illustration, the fact that A obtained a decree against C is irrelevant as between B and C. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 37: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

Q: Under what two conditions does a judgment, not covered by sections 34-36, become relevant?
A: It becomes relevant if the existence of such judgment, order, or decree is a fact in issue, or if it is relevant under some other provision of the Adhiniyam. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

Q: If A murders B because B previously got a decree to take A's land, is the decree relevant in A's murder trial?
A: Yes, the illustration states that the existence of the judgment is relevant as showing a motive for the crime, falling under the exception for relevance under other provisions. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 37: Judgments, etc., other than those mentioned in sections 34, 35 and 36 when relevant

Q: If the prosecution wants to prove a person is a repeat offender, what is the legal status of the previous conviction?
A: The illustration shows that if a person is charged with theft and with having a previous conviction for theft, the previous conviction is relevant as a fact in issue. [Source: Section 37, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: Can a party challenge a relevant judgment presented by their opponent by claiming the judge was bribed?
A: Yes, any party to a proceeding may show that a relevant judgment, order, or decree proved by the adverse party was obtained by fraud or collusion. [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: What right does Section 38 of BSA 2023 give to parties facing an adverse judgment as evidence?
A: Section 38 of BSA 2023 gives a party the right to prove that a judgment, order, or decree relevant under sections 34-36 was delivered by an incompetent Court or obtained by fraud or collusion. [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: If a plaintiff introduces a prior judgment to bar a second suit, can the defendant argue the first court had no jurisdiction?
A: Yes, the defendant may show that the judgment delivered by the Court was not competent to deliver it. [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: What are the three specific grounds on which a party can challenge a relevant judgment proved by the adverse party?
A: The three grounds are that the judgment was delivered by a Court not competent to deliver it, that it was obtained by fraud, or that it was obtained by collusion. [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: Does this section allow challenging any judgment whatsoever?
A: The section specifically refers to judgments, orders, or decrees 'which is relevant under section 34, 35 or 36, and which has been proved by the adverse party.' [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 38: Fraud or collusion in obtaining judgment, or incompetency of Court, may be proved

Q: What happens if a party successfully proves that a previous judgment was obtained by fraud?
A: The consequence is that the previous judgment's evidentiary value and binding effect (such as operating as a bar to a suit) are nullified in the current proceeding. [Source: Section 38, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: Can a person with special skills in science or handwriting give their opinion as evidence in court?
A: Yes, when the Court has to form an opinion on points of foreign law, science, art, handwriting, or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in those fields (experts) are relevant facts. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: How does Section 39 of BSA 2023 define and treat experts?
A: Section 39 of BSA 2023 defines experts as persons specially skilled in specific fields like science, art, or foreign law, and treats their opinions on those points as relevant facts. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: If a person dies of suspected poisoning, can a toxicologist testify about the symptoms that poison causes?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that the opinions of experts as to the symptoms produced by the poison are relevant facts. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: What specific fields are explicitly mentioned where expert opinion is relevant?
A: The explicitly mentioned fields are foreign law, science, art, 'any other field,' and questions as to the identity of handwriting or finger impressions. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: Is an expert's opinion required for electronic evidence stored on a computer?
A: Yes, sub-section (2) explicitly states that the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence (under the IT Act, 2000) is a relevant fact when forming an opinion on electronic information. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 39: Opinions of experts

Q: When a Court needs to determine if two documents were written by the same person, how can it use expert testimony?
A: As per the illustration, the opinions of experts on the question whether the two documents were written by the same person or different persons are legally admissible as relevant facts. [Source: Section 39, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: Can seemingly irrelevant facts be introduced in court if they back up what an expert witness is saying?
A: Yes, facts that are not otherwise relevant become relevant if they support or are inconsistent with the opinions of experts, when those opinions are relevant. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: What rule does Section 40 of BSA 2023 establish regarding facts that interact with expert opinions?
A: Section 40 of BSA 2023 establishes that otherwise irrelevant facts become relevant if they either support or contradict the relevant opinions of experts. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: If an expert claims a specific poison causes a certain rash, can the prosecution introduce evidence that other people who took the same poison also got that rash?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that the fact that other persons poisoned by the same poison exhibited those symptoms is relevant because it supports the expert's opinion. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: What are the two conditions for an otherwise irrelevant fact to become relevant under this section?
A: The fact must either support or be inconsistent with an expert's opinion, and the expert's opinion itself must be relevant to the case. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: If an expert's opinion is deemed irrelevant to the case, can a party still introduce facts to support that opinion?
A: No, the section explicitly adds the condition 'when such opinions are relevant,' meaning the underlying expert opinion must first be admissible. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 40: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts

Q: How does the law treat evidence showing that other harbours with similar sea-walls also experienced obstruction?
A: As shown in the illustration, such evidence is treated as a relevant fact because it supports an expert's opinion on whether a specific sea-wall caused a harbour's obstruction. [Source: Section 40, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 41: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant

Q: How can the Court determine if a specific person signed a document?
A: The opinion of any person who is acquainted with the handwriting of the supposed signer, stating whether it was or was not written or signed by that person, is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 41: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant

Q: What does Section 41 of BSA 2023 state about proving handwriting and electronic signatures?
A: Section 41 of BSA 2023 states that opinions of persons acquainted with the handwriting are relevant for physical documents, and the opinion of the Certifying Authority is relevant for electronic signatures. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

Q: If a clerk's job is to file correspondence from a specific merchant, but they have never actually seen the merchant write, is their opinion on the merchant's handwriting relevant?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the clerk's opinion is relevant because they habitually received documents purporting to be written by the merchant in the ordinary course of business. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 41: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant

Q: What constitutes being 'acquainted with the handwriting' of another person under this section?
A: A person is acquainted if they have seen the person write, received documents answering their own addressed to that person, or habitually received documents supposedly written by that person in the course of business. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 41: Opinion as to handwriting and signature, when relevant

Q: Is a layperson's opinion admissible to verify an electronic signature?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly requires the opinion of the Certifying Authority which issued the Electronic Signature Certificate when forming an opinion as to an electronic signature. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

Q: When a Certifying Authority provides its opinion on an electronic signature, how does the Court treat it?
A: The Court legally treats the Certifying Authority's opinion as a relevant fact when determining the authenticity of the electronic signature. [Source: Section 41, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 42: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

Q: When a dispute involves a broad custom affecting many people, whose opinion can the court consider?
A: The Court can consider the opinions of persons who would be likely to know of the existence of the general custom or right, if it actually existed. [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 42: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

Q: What rule does Section 42 of BSA 2023 establish regarding general customs or rights?
A: Section 42 of BSA 2023 establishes that opinions as to the existence of a general custom or right are relevant if given by persons likely to know of its existence. [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 42: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

Q: If the villagers of a particular village claim they have a right to use the water of a specific well, is this considered a 'general right'?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that the right of the villagers to use the water of a particular well is a general right within the meaning of this section. [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 42: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

Q: What does the expression 'general custom or right' specifically include under this section?
A: The Explanation states that the expression includes customs or rights common to any considerable class of persons. [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:

Q: Can the court accept the opinion of a random outsider who is unlikely to know about the local custom?
A: No, the section specifies that the opinions must come from 'persons who would be likely to know of its existence if it existed.' [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 42: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

Q: What evidentiary value does the opinion of a knowledgeable local elder have when determining a village custom?
A: The elder's opinion is given the evidentiary value of a relevant fact, aiding the Court in forming its conclusion about the custom's existence. [Source: Section 42, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to existence of general custom or right, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: How does a court determine the meaning of specialized local slang or religious tenets?
A: The Court may consider the opinions of persons having special means of knowledge regarding the usages, tenets, religious constitutions, or the meaning of words used in particular districts or by particular classes. [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: What does Section 43 of BSA 2023 say about proving specialized usages or meanings?
A: Section 43 of BSA 2023 says that when forming an opinion on usages, tenets, charitable foundations, or localized terms, the opinions of persons with special means of knowledge are relevant facts. [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: If a legal dispute hinges on the specific governance rules of a local charitable foundation, whose opinion is relevant?
A: The opinions of persons having special means of knowledge regarding the constitution and governance of that religious or charitable foundation are relevant facts. [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: What are the three specific categories of topics where opinions of knowledgeable persons are made relevant by this section?
A: The three categories are: (i) usages and tenets of a body of men or family; (ii) constitution and governance of religious or charitable foundations; and (iii) meaning of words or terms used in particular districts or classes. [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: Does this section permit just anyone to give their opinion on the meaning of a local dialect word?
A: No, the section specifically restricts relevant opinions to those of 'persons having special means of knowledge thereon.' [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 43: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

Q: How is the testimony of a local linguist treated when deciphering a dialect term in a contract?
A: Their testimony is treated as a relevant fact, allowing the Court to use their specialized knowledge to determine the term's meaning. [Source: Section 43, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion as to usages, tenets, etc., when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: How can the relationship between two people, like marriage or parentage, be proven in court through the opinions of others?
A: The opinion, expressed by conduct, as to the existence of such relationship by any person who has special means of knowledge (like a family member) is a relevant fact. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: What rule does Section 44 of BSA 2023 establish regarding proving relationships?
A: Section 44 of BSA 2023 establishes that an opinion regarding a relationship, expressed by conduct by someone with special means of knowledge, is relevant, but insufficient to prove marriage in certain strict proceedings. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: If a couple is usually received and treated by their friends as husband and wife, is this conduct relevant to prove they are married?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, the fact that they were usually received and treated by their friends as husband and wife is relevant as opinion expressed by conduct. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: What are the two core requirements for an opinion on a relationship to be relevant under this section?
A: The opinion must be 'expressed by conduct,' and it must come from a person who, as a family member or otherwise, has 'special means of knowledge' on the subject. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: Can the fact that a couple is treated as married by friends be used to prove bigamy under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
A: No, the proviso explicitly states that such opinion shall not be sufficient to prove a marriage in prosecutions under sections 82 and 84 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or in Divorce Act proceedings. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 44: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

Q: What legal weight is given to the fact that family members have always treated a child as the legitimate son of his father?
A: As per the illustration, this conduct is given the legal weight of a relevant fact to help form an opinion on the relationship. [Source: Section 44, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Opinion on relationship, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: If a witness is allowed to give their opinion, can they also explain the reasoning behind it?
A: Yes, whenever the opinion of any living person is relevant, the grounds on which such opinion is based are also relevant. [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: What does Section 45 of BSA 2023 dictate about the basis of a relevant opinion?
A: Section 45 of BSA 2023 dictates that whenever the opinion of any living person is deemed relevant, the specific grounds upon which that opinion is based are also relevant. [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: Can a forensic scientist who testifies about a blood match also describe the chemical tests they ran to reach that conclusion?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, an expert may give an account of experiments performed by him for the purpose of forming his opinion. [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: What is the single prerequisite for the grounds of an opinion to become relevant under this section?
A: The prerequisite is that the opinion itself of the living person must first be considered relevant under the law. [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: Does this section apply to the grounds of an opinion held by a person who is deceased?
A: No, the section specifically uses the phrase 'whenever the opinion of any living person is relevant.' [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 45: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Q: How does the admissibility of an expert's experiments affect the court's evaluation of their testimony?
A: By making the grounds relevant, the court can evaluate not just the final conclusion of the expert, but the scientific rigor and factual basis supporting that conclusion. [Source: Section 45, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grounds of opinion, when relevant

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 46: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: In a civil dispute, can a person's general character be used as evidence to prove they likely committed a specific act?
A: No, in civil cases, the fact that a person's character makes any imputed conduct probable or improbable is irrelevant, except insofar as such character appears from facts otherwise relevant. [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 46: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: What does Section 46 of BSA 2023 establish regarding character evidence in civil cases?
A: Section 46 of BSA 2023 establishes that a person's character is irrelevant in civil cases for proving that they likely committed imputed conduct. [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 46: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: If A sues B for breach of contract, can A argue that B has a reputation for being a liar to prove B broke the contract?
A: No, because in civil cases, character is irrelevant to prove that a person probably committed the conduct imputed to them. [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 46: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: What specific legal proceeding does the rule in this section apply to?
A: The rule in this section applies explicitly and exclusively to civil cases. [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 46: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: Is character completely banned from being mentioned in a civil case under any circumstances?
A: No, the section allows an exception where character is relevant 'in so far as such character appears from facts otherwise relevant.' [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In civil cases character to prove conduct imputed, irrelevant

Q: What happens if a lawyer tries to introduce a witness solely to testify about the opposing party's bad character in a property dispute?
A: The testimony will be deemed irrelevant and excluded from evidence, as character cannot be used to prove imputed conduct in civil cases. [Source: Section 46, BSA 2023]

Q: In a criminal trial, can the accused present evidence showing they are generally a good, law-abiding person?
A: Yes, in criminal proceedings, the fact that the person accused is of a good character is relevant. [Source: Section 47, BSA 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 47: In criminal cases previous good character relevant

Q: What does Section 47 of BSA 2023 state about an accused person's character?
A: Section 47 of BSA 2023 states simply that in criminal proceedings, the previous good character of the person accused is relevant. [Source: Section 47, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In criminal cases previous good character relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 47: In criminal cases previous good character relevant

Q: If a person with no prior record is accused of theft, can their lawyer call witnesses to testify about their lifelong honesty?
A: Yes, because the fact that the accused person is of a good character is legally relevant in criminal proceedings. [Source: Section 47, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: In criminal cases previous good character relevant

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 47: In criminal cases previous good character relevant

A: The proceeding must be a criminal proceeding, and the evidence must relate to the 'good character' of the person accused. [Source: Section 47, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 48: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases

Q: In a trial for sexual assault, can the defense use the victim's past sexual history to argue they consented?
A: No, where the question of consent is in issue in prosecutions for specified sexual offences, evidence of the victim's character or previous sexual experience with any person shall not be relevant on the issue of consent. [Source: Section 48, BSA 2023]

content:

Q: What restriction does Section 48 of BSA 2023 place on evidence in sexual offence cases?
A: Section 48 of BSA 2023 restricts the use of evidence regarding the victim's character or previous sexual experience, stating it is not relevant on the issue of consent or the quality of consent. [Source: Section 48, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 48: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases

Q: If an accused claims a rape victim consented because she had a reputation for promiscuity, is that reputation admissible?
A: No, evidence of the character of the victim is strictly declared not relevant on the issue of consent or the quality of consent. [Source: Section 48, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 49: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

Q: Can the prosecution in a criminal trial introduce evidence that the accused is a bad person with a criminal past?
A: Generally no, the fact that the accused has a bad character is irrelevant, unless evidence has been given that he has a good character, in which case the bad character becomes relevant in reply. [Source: Section 49, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 49: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

Q: What rule does Section 49 of BSA 2023 establish regarding bad character evidence in criminal proceedings?
A: Section 49 of BSA 2023 establishes that previous bad character is irrelevant unless the accused introduces evidence of good character, or if the bad character is itself a fact in issue. [Source: Section 49, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 49: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

A: Yes, because evidence has been given that the accused has a good character, evidence of bad character becomes relevant in reply. [Source: Section 49, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 49: Previous bad character not relevant, except in reply

Q: What specific event must occur during a trial before the prosecution can introduce evidence of bad character?
A: Evidence must first have been given that the accused has a good character. [Source: Section 49, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: In a civil lawsuit seeking financial compensation, can a person's character be considered when deciding how much money they should get?
A: Yes, in civil cases, the fact that the character of any person is such as to affect the amount of damages which he ought to receive is relevant. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Character as affecting damages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: What does Section 50 of BSA 2023 state about character and damages?
A: Section 50 of BSA 2023 states that in civil cases, a person's character is a relevant fact if it affects the amount of damages they ought to receive. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Character as affecting damages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: If a person sues a newspaper for defamation claiming their pristine reputation was ruined, can the newspaper introduce evidence that the person already had a terrible reputation?
A: Yes, because the person's prior reputation affects the amount of damages they ought to receive for the defamation. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Character as affecting damages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: How does the Explanation define the word 'character' for the purposes of this and related sections?
A: The Explanation states that the word 'character' includes both reputation and disposition. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Character as affecting damages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: When providing evidence of character under this section, can a party list specific bad things the person did in the past?
A: No, the Explanation specifies that evidence may be given only of general reputation and general disposition, and not of particular acts by which reputation or disposition has been shown. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Character as affecting damages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 50: Character as affecting damages

Q: How does character evidence function legally in a damages suit compared to a suit to prove liability?
A: While character is irrelevant to prove conduct or liability in civil cases (under Section 46), it becomes a relevant fact under this section solely for the purpose of calculating the appropriate amount of damages. [Source: Section 50, BSA 2023]

A: Section 51 of BSA 2023 establishes that facts which are judicially noticeable do not need to be proved by evidence in court. [Source: Section 51, BSA 2023]

A: Yes, because it is a fact of which the Court will take judicial notice, and therefore it need not be proved. [Source: Section 51, BSA 2023]

Q: Does a lawyer have to bring a copy of a widely known law to prove that it exists?
A: No, because the Court shall take judicial notice of all laws in force in the territory of India, including those having extra-territorial operation. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

Q: What does Section 52 of BSA 2023 list?
A: Section 52 of BSA 2023 lists specific facts of which the Court shall take judicial notice, such as laws, international treaties, the territory of India, and public holidays. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 52: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

Q: If a court is asked to recognize that a war started between India and another country, must evidence be presented to prove the war exists?
A: No, because the Court shall take judicial notice of the commencement, continuance, and termination of hostilities between the Government of India and any other country. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 52: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

Q: What must a person do if they want the Court to take judicial notice of a matter of public history or literature?
A: Under sub-section (2), the Court may refuse to take judicial notice of any fact unless and until the person produces an appropriate book or document of reference that the Court considers necessary. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 52: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

Q: Are all government officers automatically judicially noticed by the Court without any specific requirements?
A: No, under clause (f), the Court takes judicial notice of persons filling a public office only if the fact of their appointment is notified in any Official Gazette. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 52: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

Q: What is the legal effect when a country is recognized as sovereign by the Government of India?
A: The consequence is that the Court shall automatically take judicial notice of the existence, title, and national flag of that country. [Source: Section 52, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts of which Court shall take judicial notice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: If both parties in a lawsuit agree on a specific fact, do they still have to present evidence to prove it to the judge?
A: No, no fact needs to be proved in any proceeding which the parties or their agents agree to admit at the hearing, or have admitted in writing before the hearing or in their pleadings. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: What rule does Section 53 of BSA 2023 lay down regarding admitted facts?
A: Section 53 of BSA 2023 lays down that facts admitted by parties or their agents at or before the hearing, or in their pleadings, do not need to be proved. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: If a defendant writes a letter to the plaintiff before trial admitting they owe $5,000, does the plaintiff need to prove the debt exists during the hearing?
A: No, because it is a fact which before the hearing they agreed to admit by a writing under their hands. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: What are the three ways a fact can be admitted under this section so that it doesn't need to be proved?
A: It can be admitted at the hearing, agreed to be admitted by writing before the hearing, or deemed to have been admitted by the rules of pleading in force. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: Is the Court absolutely forced to accept an admitted fact without any proof?
A: No, the proviso states that the Court may, in its discretion, require the facts admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admissions. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 53: Facts admitted need not be proved

Q: What happens procedurally when a fact is deemed to have been admitted by the pleadings?
A: The consequence is that the fact generally no longer requires formal proof during the proceeding, unless the Court uses its discretion to require it. [Source: Section 53, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Facts admitted need not be proved

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: Can spoken testimony be used to prove almost any fact in a court case?
A: Yes, all facts, except the contents of documents, may be proved by oral evidence. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: What is the core principle of Section 54 of BSA 2023 regarding oral evidence?
A: The core principle of Section 54 of BSA 2023 is that oral evidence is permissible to prove all facts, with the explicit exception of the contents of documents. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: If someone wants to prove that it was raining on the day of a robbery, can they do so by calling a witness to simply state that it was raining?
A: Yes, because all facts, except the contents of documents, may be proved by oral evidence. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: What is the single category of facts specifically excluded from being proved by oral evidence under this section?
A: The contents of documents are the only facts specifically excluded from being proved by oral evidence under this section. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: Does this section provide any exception allowing the contents of documents to be proved by oral evidence?
A: No, this specific section states an absolute rule that all facts 'except the contents of documents' may be proved by oral evidence. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 54: Proof of facts by oral evidence

Q: If a party attempts to prove what was written in a contract solely by having someone recite it from memory on the stand, what will happen under this rule?
A: The oral testimony will likely be rejected for that purpose, as the section forbids proving the contents of documents by oral evidence. [Source: Section 54, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of facts by oral evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: Can a witness testify about something they heard about from someone else, rather than seeing it themselves?
A: No, oral evidence must in all cases be direct; if it refers to a fact which could be seen, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he saw it. [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: What strict requirement does Section 55 of BSA 2023 place on oral evidence?
A: Section 55 of BSA 2023 requires that oral evidence must be direct, meaning it must come from the person who directly perceived the fact with their own senses or who holds the opinion being presented. [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: If a witness says, 'My friend told me he heard a gunshot,' can this be used as oral evidence to prove the gunshot happened?
A: No, because oral evidence must be direct; if it refers to a fact which could be heard, it must be the evidence of a witness who says he actually heard it. [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: What are the four specific categories of facts for which oral evidence must be direct under this section?
A: The four categories are: facts which could be seen, facts which could be heard, facts perceived by any other sense, and opinions (or the grounds for opinions). [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: Is there any situation where an expert's opinion can be introduced without the expert testifying in person?
A: Yes, the first proviso states that opinions of experts expressed in a commonly sold treatise may be proved by producing the treatise if the author is dead, cannot be found, or is unreasonably delayed or expensive to call. [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 55: Oral evidence to be direct

Q: If oral evidence refers to the condition of a physical weapon (a material thing), what power does the Court have?
A: The second proviso gives the Court the power to require the production of that material thing for its inspection, if it thinks fit. [Source: Section 55, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Oral evidence to be direct

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: In what ways can a person legally prove what is written inside a document?
A: The contents of documents may be proved either by primary or by secondary evidence. [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: What does Section 56 of BSA 2023 state about proving the contents of documents?
A: Section 56 of BSA 2023 states simply that the contents of documents may be proved either by primary or by secondary evidence. [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: If a lawyer wants to show the court what a contract says, but the original contract is lost, can they use a photocopy instead?
A: Yes, because the contents of documents may be proved by secondary evidence (like a photocopy) if primary evidence is not available. [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: What are the two mutually exclusive categories of evidence permitted by this section to prove document contents?
A: The two categories are primary evidence and secondary evidence. [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: Can a witness just summarize what a document said from memory as a third alternative to primary or secondary evidence?
A: No, the section restricts the proof of contents of documents strictly to either primary or secondary evidence (though some oral accounts count as secondary evidence under specific rules). [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 56: Proof of contents of documents

Q: By defining these two categories, what fundamental rule of evidence does this section establish for documentary proof?
A: It establishes that any attempt to prove a document's contents must legally qualify as either primary or secondary evidence to be admissible in court. [Source: Section 56, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of contents of documents

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: What is the highest form of evidence to prove a document in court?
A: Primary evidence, which means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: How does Section 57 of BSA 2023 define primary evidence?
A: Section 57 of BSA 2023 defines primary evidence as the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court, and includes specific rules for multi-part, counterpart, and electronic documents. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: If ten identical posters are printed from a single digital file, is one of the posters primary evidence of what the other nine posters say?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, because they are all made by one uniform process (printing), any one of the placards is primary evidence of the contents of any other. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: Under Explanation 4, if a digital record is stored simultaneously in multiple files, how are those files classified?
A: Each such file is classified as primary evidence. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: If fifty copies of a hand-written letter are made using a photocopier, are those photocopies primary evidence of the original hand-written letter?
A: No, Explanation 3 states that where they are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 57: Primary evidence

Q: What is the legal status of an electronic record produced from proper custody if no one challenges its authenticity?
A: Under Explanation 5, such an electronic and digital record is treated as primary evidence unless it is disputed. [Source: Section 57, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: What types of evidence count as secondary evidence when the original document cannot be produced?
A: Secondary evidence includes certified copies, mechanical copies ensuring accuracy, copies compared with the original, counterparts against non-executing parties, oral accounts by someone who saw the original, and written/oral admissions. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: What does Section 58 of BSA 2023 list as secondary evidence?
A: Section 58 of BSA 2023 lists eight specific categories of secondary evidence, including certified copies, copies made by mechanical processes, oral accounts of someone who saw the original, and admissions. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: If a person takes a photograph of a contract, can that photograph be used as secondary evidence?
A: Yes, the illustration confirms that a photograph of an original is secondary evidence of its contents, provided it is proved that the thing photographed was the original. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: What specific condition must a mechanical copy meet to be considered secondary evidence under clause (ii)?
A: The copy must be made by a mechanical process which in itself ensures the accuracy of the copy. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: Is an oral account of a photocopy considered secondary evidence of the original document?
A: No, the illustration explicitly states that neither an oral account of a copy compared with the original, nor an oral account of a photograph or machine-copy of the original, is secondary evidence of the original. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 58: Secondary evidence

Q: How does the law treat the testimony of a skilled accountant who examined numerous complex ledgers that cannot be brought to court?
A: Under clause (viii), their evidence regarding the general result of those documents is legally admitted as secondary evidence. [Source: Section 58, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Secondary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: What is the default rule for proving a document in court?
A: Documents shall be proved by primary evidence except in the specific cases mentioned in subsequent sections. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: What strict general rule does Section 59 of BSA 2023 establish?
A: Section 59 of BSA 2023 establishes the general rule that documents must be proved by primary evidence, subject only to specific exceptions. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: A lawyer has a perfectly clear photocopy of a contract and wants to submit it to save the trouble of finding the original. Is this allowed as a first choice?
A: No, because documents shall be proved by primary evidence except in specified exceptional cases. The original must be produced if possible. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: What type of evidence is mandatory under this section for proving a document?
A: Primary evidence is the mandatory type of evidence for proving a document under this section. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: Does this section absolutely ban the use of secondary evidence?
A: No, the section includes the caveat 'except in the cases hereinafter mentioned,' acknowledging that secondary evidence is permitted under specific conditions. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 59: Proof of documents by primary evidence

Q: What happens to a case if a party attempts to prove a document using secondary evidence but fails to prove they meet any of the allowed exceptions?
A: The secondary evidence will be rejected by the court because the default requirement to use primary evidence has not been legally bypassed. [Source: Section 59, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of documents by primary evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: When is a party allowed to use a copy of a document instead of the original in court?
A: Secondary evidence may be given when the original is lost, destroyed, in the opponent's possession, not easily movable, a public document, or consists of numerous accounts that are hard to examine in court. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: What exceptions are listed in Section 60 of BSA 2023?
A: Section 60 of BSA 2023 lists the specific cases where secondary evidence may be given, such as when the original is lost, destroyed, in the adversary's control, or is a public document. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: If the original deed to a house was destroyed in a fire without the owner's fault, can the owner use secondary evidence?
A: Yes, secondary evidence is allowed when the original has been destroyed or lost, or cannot be produced in reasonable time for reasons not arising from the party's own default or neglect. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: Under clause (a), what three locations or persons possessing the original document justify the use of secondary evidence after notice is given?
A: The original must be in the possession of (i) the opposing party, (ii) a person out of the Court's reach, or (iii) any person legally bound to produce it. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: If the original is a public document, can a party bring an oral witness to testify about its contents as secondary evidence?
A: No, the Explanation clarifies that for public documents (clause e), a certified copy of the document, but 'no other kind of secondary evidence,' is admissible. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 60: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

Q: What is the legal effect when a party successfully proves the opposing party admitted to the contents of a document in writing?
A: Under clause (b) and its Explanation, the written admission itself becomes admissible as secondary evidence of the document's contents. [Source: Section 60, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases in which secondary evidence relating to documents may be given

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record

Q: Can a piece of evidence be rejected simply because it is in a digital format?
A: No, nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record solely on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record. [Source: Section 61, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Electronic or digital record

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record

Q: What does Section 61 of BSA 2023 establish about the legal effect of digital records?
A: Section 61 of BSA 2023 establishes that, subject to section 63, an electronic or digital record shall have the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as any other document. [Source: Section 61, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Electronic or digital record

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record

Q: If a lawyer tries to exclude an email from evidence arguing that 'emails aren't real paper documents,' will the court agree?
A: No, because the section explicitly prohibits denying admissibility on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record. [Source: Section 61, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Electronic or digital record

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record

Q: What specific condition limits the equal legal effect granted to electronic records under this section?
A: The equal legal effect, validity, and enforceability are granted 'subject to section 63.' [Source: Section 61, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Electronic or digital record

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record

Q: Does this section guarantee that every digital record will be automatically admitted into evidence?
A: No, it only states that it cannot be denied solely for being digital; it must still satisfy the rules of admissibility, notably those in section 63. [Source: Section 61, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Electronic or digital record

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 61: Electronic or digital record
