A: Yes, the Court may presume that any published map or chart produced for inspection was written and published by the person, and at the time and place, by whom or at which it purports to be. [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 89: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

Q: What presumption does Section 89 of BSA 2023 create for reference materials?
A: Section 89 of BSA 2023 creates a discretionary presumption that books on matters of public interest, maps, and charts were actually written and published by the persons and at the times/places they claim. [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 89: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

Q: A historian submits a 19th-century book on local customs. It says 'Printed by Smith in London, 1850.' Must the historian prove Smith actually printed it then?
A: No, the Court may presume the book was published by the person (Smith), and at the time (1850) and place (London), by whom or at which it purports to have been published. [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 89: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

Q: What specific type of subject matter must a 'book' contain for the Court to refer to it under this section?
A: It must be a book referred to for information on 'matters of public or general interest.' [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 89: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

Q: Does this section presume that the actual facts written inside the history book or map are 100% accurate and true?
A: No, it only allows the court to presume the document 'was written and published by the person, and at the time and place' it claims; the accuracy of the contents is a separate evidentiary issue. [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 89: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

Q: What practical evidentiary burden does this section relieve when dealing with standard published works?
A: It relieves parties from the impossible burden of proving the authorship and publication details of old or widely distributed public reference materials. [Source: Section 89, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to books, maps and charts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: If you send an email, does the court assume the email received by the other person is exactly what you typed?
A: Yes, the Court may presume that an electronic message forwarded through an electronic mail server corresponds exactly with the message as fed into the sender's computer for transmission. [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: What does Section 90 of BSA 2023 say about electronic messages?
A: Section 90 of BSA 2023 says courts may presume an electronic message received matches the one sent, but shall not presume who actually sent it. [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: Bob receives a threatening email purporting to be from Alice's account. The court presumes the text wasn't altered in transit. Can the court also automatically presume Alice typed it?
A: No, the section explicitly states 'the Court shall not make any presumption as to the person by whom such message was sent.' [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: Through what specific technological intermediary must the message be forwarded for this presumption to apply?
A: The message must be forwarded 'through an electronic mail server.' [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: Is the court forced to presume the transmitted email is identical to the typed email in every single case?
A: No, the section states the Court 'may presume,' meaning it is a discretionary presumption that the court can choose not to apply if circumstances warrant suspicion. [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 90: Presumption as to electronic messages

Q: What critical evidentiary gap does the negative presumption (not presuming the sender) leave for the party submitting the email?
A: The party must independently prove the identity of the person who actually hit 'send' or typed the message, separate from proving the message text itself. [Source: Section 90, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic messages

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: If a party refuses to bring a requested document to court, what does the judge assume about that hidden document?
A: The Court shall presume that every document called for and not produced after notice to produce was properly attested, stamped, and executed in the manner required by law. [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: What presumption does Section 91 of BSA 2023 create against a party who withholds a document?
A: Section 91 of BSA 2023 creates the presumption that a document not produced after a notice to produce was legally attested, stamped, and executed. [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: A defendant refuses to produce a contract after receiving a legal notice. They later argue the contract was invalid because it lacked a required stamp. Will the court accept this argument?
A: No, because the Court shall presume that the document not produced was legally stamped and executed. [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: What specific procedural step must be completed before the court makes this presumption against the non-producing party?
A: The document must have been called for and not produced 'after notice to produce.' [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: If a party simply forgets to bring a document they weren't formally asked for, does this negative presumption automatically apply?
A: No, the presumption strictly applies to documents not produced 'after notice to produce.' [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 91: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

Q: By making this presumption, how does the law penalize parties who try to hide evidence?
A: It prevents them from taking advantage of their own refusal by stripping away their ability to claim the hidden document was procedurally flawed or invalid. [Source: Section 91, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to due execution, etc., of documents not produced

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: Does a party have to find a living witness to prove the signature on a 40-year-old property deed?
A: No, if a document is thirty years old and produced from proper custody, the Court may presume that the handwriting and signatures belong to the purported persons and that it was duly executed. [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: What does Section 92 of BSA 2023 state about very old documents?
A: Section 92 of BSA 2023 states that the Court may presume the genuineness of handwriting, signatures, and execution for documents that are at least thirty years old and come from proper custody. [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: A grandchild finds a 35-year-old handwritten letter in their grandfather's locked desk. Will the court require a handwriting expert to prove the grandfather wrote it?
A: Not necessarily; because it is over thirty years old and from proper custody (his desk), the Court may presume it is in his handwriting. [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: What is the exact minimum age a document must purport or be proved to be to trigger this specific presumption?
A: The document must be 'thirty years old.' [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: Is the court absolutely required to assume every 30-year-old document is genuine?
A: No, the section states the Court 'may presume,' making it a discretionary presumption that the court can choose not to apply if it has doubts. [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 92: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

Q: What practical evidentiary barrier does this rule overcome in historical property or contract disputes?
A: It overcomes the impossibility of proving documents when all the original signatories, witnesses, and authors have long since passed away. [Source: Section 92, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to documents thirty years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: How old does an electronic record have to be before a court can automatically presume its digital signature is genuine?
A: The electronic record must purport or be proved to be five years old, and be produced from proper custody, for the Court to presume the digital signature was affixed by the authorized person. [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: What special presumption does Section 93 of BSA 2023 grant to older electronic records?
A: Section 93 of BSA 2023 grants a discretionary presumption that the electronic signature on an electronic record at least five years old (from proper custody) was affixed by the purported person. [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: A company retrieves a digitally signed PDF contract from its secure server archive that is dated six years ago. Does it need to prove the other party clicked 'sign'?
A: The Court may presume the electronic signature was affixed by that person, because the record is over five years old and from proper custody. [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: What are the two main conditions an electronic record must meet for this section to apply?
A: It must be 'five years old' and produced from 'any custody which the Court in the particular case considers proper.' [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: Is this 5-year rule for electronic records an absolute mandate that the court must follow?
A: No, it is a discretionary presumption, as indicated by the phrase 'the Court may presume'. [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 93: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

Q: Why does the law set the age for presumption at 5 years for electronic records, compared to 30 years for physical documents?
A: It recognizes the rapid pace of technological change and the transient nature of digital data, making it difficult to find technical witnesses or logs for older digital events. [Source: Section 93, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to electronic records five years old

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: If two parties write down their contract in a formal document, can one of them later bring a witness to testify that the actual terms were different?
A: No, when the terms of a contract have been reduced to a document, no evidence shall be given to prove the terms except the document itself (or secondary evidence if permitted). [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: What fundamental evidentiary rule is established by Section 94 of BSA 2023 regarding written contracts?
A: Section 94 of BSA 2023 establishes the rule that when a contract or property disposition is written down, the document itself is the only admissible proof of its terms, excluding oral testimony about those terms. [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: A landlord and tenant sign a written lease. The tenant later claims the landlord verbally promised free electricity during the signing. Will the court hear this claim?
A: No, because the terms were reduced to a document, and no outside evidence can be given to prove the terms of the contract. [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: What three types of legal transactions does this section explicitly list as being subject to this exclusionary rule when written down?
A: The rule applies to the terms of a 'contract,' a 'grant,' or 'any other disposition of property.' [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: If a written contract mentions in passing that a completely separate, unrelated verbal payment happened last week, can a party offer oral evidence about that past payment?
A: Yes, Explanation 3 states that a statement of a fact other than the terms of the contract shall not preclude the admission of oral evidence as to that same fact. [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 94: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

Q: What legal certainty does this section provide to parties engaging in formal written transactions?
A: It provides certainty that the written text they agree to will be the final, binding word in court, immune from later contradiction by 'he-said, she-said' oral claims. [Source: Section 94, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence of terms of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: Once a written contract is proven in court, can a party introduce evidence of a prior secret verbal agreement that contradicts the written text?
A: No, no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted between the parties to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the terms of the written document. [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: What prohibition does Section 95 of BSA 2023 place on oral agreements relating to written contracts?
A: Section 95 of BSA 2023 prohibits admitting evidence of oral agreements intended to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the terms of a proven written contract. [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: A buys a car from B with a written contract stating the price is fixed at 1 lakh. Can A later testify that B verbally promised a 10% discount if A paid in cash?
A: No, A cannot introduce evidence of an oral agreement to vary or subtract from the written terms of the contract. [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: According to the second proviso, what two conditions must a separate oral agreement meet to be admissible despite the written contract?
A: The oral agreement must be on a matter 'on which a document is silent' and it must be 'not inconsistent with its terms.' [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: Can a party introduce oral evidence to prove they were forced to sign the written contract at gunpoint?
A: Yes, the first proviso explicitly allows proving any fact that would invalidate the document, such as fraud, intimidation, or illegality. [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 95: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

Q: How does the fourth proviso accommodate situations where parties change their minds long after signing a written contract?
A: It allows evidence of a 'distinct subsequent oral agreement to rescind or modify' the contract, provided the law doesn't explicitly require that specific type of contract to be in writing. [Source: Section 95, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: If a contract has blank spaces or uses confusing language that contradicts itself, can the parties testify about what they actually meant to write?
A: No, when the language used in a document is, on its face, ambiguous or defective, evidence may not be given of facts which would show its meaning or supply its defects. [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: What rule does Section 96 of BSA 2023 establish regarding patent ambiguities in documents?
A: Section 96 of BSA 2023 establishes that if a document's language is ambiguous or defective on its face, no outside evidence can be admitted to explain its meaning or fill its defects. [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: A deed states a property is sold for 'one lakh or two lakh rupees.' Can the buyer bring a witness to testify that they verbally agreed on one lakh before signing?
A: No, because the language is ambiguous on its face, and evidence cannot be given to show which price was to be given. [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: What two specific flaws in the language used in a document trigger the exclusion of explanatory evidence under this section?
A: The language must be, on its face, 'ambiguous' or 'defective.' [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: If a document is perfectly clear, but outside circumstances make it confusing to apply, does this section block evidence to clear up the confusion?
A: No, this section only applies to language that is ambiguous or defective 'on its face' (patent ambiguity), not to latent ambiguities. [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 96: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

Q: What happens to a contract that is so fundamentally defective on its face that it cannot be understood without outside evidence?
A: Because outside evidence is barred, the defective parts of the contract (or the contract as a whole) will likely be deemed void for uncertainty, as the court cannot rewrite it for the parties. [Source: Section 96, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence to explain or amend ambiguous document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: If a contract perfectly describes an existing piece of property, can the seller later claim they actually meant to sell a different piece of property?
A: No, when language used in a document is plain in itself and applies accurately to existing facts, evidence may not be given to show that it was not meant to apply to such facts. [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: What does Section 97 of BSA 2023 state about perfectly clear documents?
A: Section 97 of BSA 2023 states that if a document's language is plain and applies accurately to existing facts, no evidence can be introduced to claim the document was meant to apply to something else. [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: A sells 'my red car, license plate 1234.' A actually owns that exact car. Can A later bring evidence showing they verbally agreed to sell their blue car instead?
A: No, because the language is plain and applies accurately to existing facts (the red car), so evidence may not be given to show it was meant to apply to different facts. [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: What two conditions must be met regarding the language of the document for this exclusion rule to apply?
A: The language must be 'plain in itself' and it must apply 'accurately to existing facts.' [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: Does this section prevent a party from proving they were defrauded into writing that perfectly clear description?
A: No, the provisos under Section 95 (like fraud or mistake) still apply to invalidate a document; Section 97 simply prevents claiming a clear, valid description was intended for an entirely different object. [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 97: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

Q: How does this rule protect the integrity of written agreements?
A: It stops parties from using oral testimony to entirely subvert the plain, objectively accurate meaning of the words they chose to put in writing. [Source: Section 97, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exclusion of evidence against application of document to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: What happens if a contract clearly describes something, but that thing doesn't actually exist in reality?
A: When language is plain in itself but is unmeaning in reference to existing facts, evidence may be given to show that it was used in a peculiar sense. [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: What rule does Section 98 of BSA 2023 provide for latent ambiguities?
A: Section 98 of BSA 2023 provides that if a document's language is plain but makes no sense when applied to real-world facts, evidence can be introduced to show it was used in a peculiar or specific sense. [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: A sells B 'my house in Kolkata.' A doesn't own a house in Kolkata, but does own one in Howrah where B is already living. Can B prove the deed meant the Howrah house?
A: Yes, because the phrase is unmeaning in reference to existing facts, evidence may be given to show it was used in a peculiar sense to mean the Howrah house. [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: For this rule to allow outside evidence, what must be true about the document's language in contrast to the real-world facts?
A: The language must be 'plain in itself, but is unmeaning in reference to existing facts.' [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: If the language is confusing on its face (e.g., 'I sell some house somewhere'), does this section allow evidence to fix it?
A: No, that would be a patent ambiguity blocked by Section 96; Section 98 only applies when the language is 'plain in itself' but becomes unmeaning only when applied to the facts. [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 98: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

Q: How does this section help enforce contracts that have technical errors in descriptions?
A: It prevents contracts from failing due to misdescriptions or nicknames by allowing the court to hear evidence connecting the plain words to the parties' actual, peculiar intended meaning. [Source: Section 98, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to document unmeaning in reference to existing facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: If a contract says 'I sell my white horse,' but the seller owns two white horses, how does the court decide which one was sold?
A: Evidence may be given of facts which show which of those persons or things the language was intended to apply to. [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: What does Section 99 of BSA 2023 allow when a description fits multiple objects equally well?
A: Section 99 of BSA 2023 allows evidence to be given to show which specific person or thing the language was intended to apply to, when the language could apply to more than one. [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: A contract requires delivery of goods to 'Ramgarh.' There are towns named Ramgarh in both Rajasthan and Uttarakhand. Can the parties testify about which one they meant?
A: Yes, evidence may be given of facts showing whether Ramgarh in Rajasthan or Ramgarh in Uttarakhand was meant. [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: What specific real-world factual situation triggers the application of this section?
A: The situation where the language used 'might have been meant to apply to any one, and could not have been meant to apply to more than one, of several persons or things.' [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: If the contract says 'I sell all my white horses,' does this section apply to figure out which one they meant?
A: No, because the language 'could not have been meant to apply to more than one' is a condition for this section; 'all my white horses' clearly applies to multiple. [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 99: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

Q: What type of ambiguity does this section resolve?
A: It resolves a specific type of latent ambiguity where a perfectly plain description turns out to have multiple equally valid targets in the real world. [Source: Section 99, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language which can apply to one only of several persons

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: What happens if a contract description is half-right about one property and half-right about another property?
A: When the language applies partly to one set of facts and partly to another, but the whole does not apply correctly to either, evidence may be given to show which of the two it was meant to apply to. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: What evidentiary rule does Section 100 of BSA 2023 establish for partially incorrect descriptions?
A: Section 100 of BSA 2023 establishes that if a description is split between two different sets of existing facts but perfectly fits neither, evidence can be used to prove which set of facts was actually intended. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: A deed sells 'my land at X occupied by Y.' A owns land at X (but Z lives there), and A owns land occupied by Y (but it's at W). Can they use evidence to clarify the sale?
A: Yes, evidence may be given of facts showing which of the two properties he actually meant to sell. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: For this section to apply, the language used must apply 'partly' to one set of facts and partly to another, but what must be true about the 'whole' of the language?
A: The whole of the language must 'not apply correctly to either' set of existing facts. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: If the language perfectly matches one property and partially matches another, does this section apply?
A: No, if it perfectly matches one, Section 97 would likely apply to exclude evidence; Section 100 specifically requires that the whole does *not* apply correctly to either. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 100: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

Q: By allowing this evidence, what legal doctrine is the court applying to save the contract?
A: The court is applying a doctrine of resolving latent ambiguity by striking out the erroneous part of the description (the false demonstration) to give effect to the parties' true intention. [Source: Section 100, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to application of language to one of two sets of facts, to neither of which the whole correctly applies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: If a contract uses industry slang or extremely messy handwriting, can a party bring an expert to explain what it says?
A: Yes, evidence may be given to show the meaning of illegible characters, technical or local expressions, abbreviations, and words used in a peculiar sense. [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: What does Section 101 of BSA 2023 allow regarding difficult-to-read or specialized language in documents?
A: Section 101 of BSA 2023 allows evidence to be given to explain illegible characters, foreign, obsolete, technical, local, and regional expressions, or abbreviations. [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: A sculptor's contract says 'I sell all my mods.' Can they bring witnesses to explain whether 'mods' meant clay models or metal modelling tools in their specific industry?
A: Yes, according to the illustration, evidence may be given to show which he meant to sell, as it is an abbreviation or peculiar expression. [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: Name three specific types of 'expressions' listed in this section that can be explained by outside evidence.
A: The section lists foreign, obsolete, technical, local, and regional expressions. [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: Can a party use this section to introduce evidence completely changing the meaning of plain, commonly understood English words?
A: No, this section specifically applies to words that are illegible, not commonly intelligible, foreign, obsolete, technical, local/regional, abbreviations, or 'used in a peculiar sense.' [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 101: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

Q: How does this section help courts deal with specialized commercial or regional contracts?
A: It prevents the court from having to guess or invalidate contracts just because they use jargon, slang, or abbreviations understood by the parties but not by the general public. [Source: Section 101, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to meaning of illegible characters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: Can someone who isn't a party to a written contract testify that the parties actually made a secret verbal deal that changes the contract?
A: Yes, persons who are not parties to a document, or their representatives in interest, may give evidence of facts tending to show a contemporaneous agreement varying the terms. [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: What exception to the parol evidence rule does Section 102 of BSA 2023 create?
A: Section 102 of BSA 2023 creates an exception allowing third parties (non-parties to the document) to give evidence of oral agreements that vary the terms of a written document. [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: A and B write a contract for cash-on-delivery, but secretly agree verbally to a 3-month credit. If C's legal interests are affected by this secret credit deal, can C prove it in court?
A: Yes, while A and B cannot prove this secret deal against each other (under Section 95), C may show it because C is not a party to the document. [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: Who exactly is granted the right to give this varying evidence under this section?
A: 'Persons who are not parties to a document, or their representatives in interest.' [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: If A and B sign a contract, can A's legal representative (who steps into A's shoes after A dies) use this section to vary the terms?
A: No, because they are representatives in interest of a *party* to the document, and the section only empowers non-parties or their representatives. [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 102: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

Q: What kind of fraudulent behavior between contracting parties does this section help prevent?
A: It prevents two parties from using a fake written contract to defraud or mislead a third party, by allowing the third party to expose the true, secret verbal agreement. [Source: Section 102, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may give evidence of agreement varying terms of document

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: Do the evidentiary rules in Chapter VI override the specific rules about interpreting wills found in the Indian Succession Act?
A: No, nothing in this Chapter shall be taken to affect any of the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 as to the construction of wills. [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: What saving clause is provided by Section 103 of BSA 2023?
A: Section 103 of BSA 2023 provides a saving clause ensuring that the chapter's rules do not affect the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 regarding the construction of wills. [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: A judge is trying to interpret an ambiguous clause in a written will. Should they rely primarily on the BSA's rules for ambiguous documents or the Indian Succession Act?
A: They must respect the Indian Succession Act, 1925, because Section 103 explicitly states the BSA's chapter shall not affect its provisions regarding the construction of wills. [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: Which specific external statute is protected from interference by this chapter?
A: The 'Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925)' is protected. [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: Does this saving clause mean the Indian Succession Act overrides the BSA for the interpretation of commercial contracts?
A: No, it strictly applies only to provisions 'as to the construction of wills.' [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 103: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

Q: How does this section resolve potential conflicts between general evidence law and specific inheritance law?
A: It establishes the supremacy of the specific inheritance law (Indian Succession Act) over the general evidentiary rules of the BSA when interpreting the contents of a will. [Source: Section 103, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving of provisions of Indian Succession Act relating to wills

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: In a court case, whose job is it to actually prove that the underlying facts of the case are true?
A: Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist. [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: How does Section 104 of BSA 2023 define the 'burden of proof'?
A: Section 104 of BSA 2023 states that when a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact to get a judgment in their favor, the 'burden of proof' lies on that person. [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: A goes to court and asks the judge to punish B for theft. Who has the burden of proving the theft happened?
A: A must prove that B committed the crime, because A desires the Court to give judgment based on facts A asserts. [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: What two specific types of legal outcomes must a person be seeking to trigger their burden to prove the asserting facts?
A: They must be desiring a judgment as to any 'legal right' or 'liability.' [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: Can a plaintiff just assert a fact and force the defendant to prove it's false?
A: No, the person who 'asserts' the facts and desires the judgment 'must prove that those facts exist.' [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 104: Burden of proof

Q: What is the fundamental legal maxim enshrined in this section regarding making claims in court?
A: It enshrines the maxim that 'he who asserts must prove' (onus probandi), establishing the baseline responsibility for moving a case forward. [Source: Section 104, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: If a trial happens and absolutely neither side presents any evidence, who loses the case?
A: The person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side is the one on whom the burden of proof lies. [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: What practical test does Section 105 of BSA 2023 provide for determining who has the burden of proof?
A: Section 105 of BSA 2023 provides that the burden of proof lies on the person who would fail the suit or proceeding if no evidence at all were given on either side. [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: A sues B for a debt, and B admits signing the loan contract but claims they were tricked by fraud. If neither side presents any evidence at the trial, who loses?
A: B would lose (fail), because the bond is admitted and fraud isn't proven. Therefore, the burden of proof to show fraud is on B. [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: What hypothetical scenario must the Court consider to determine where the burden of proof lies under this section?
A: The Court must consider the hypothetical scenario where 'no evidence at all were given on either side.' [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: Does the burden of proof always remain entirely on the plaintiff who started the lawsuit?
A: No, the burden can shift to the defendant depending on the pleadings (like in the fraud example), as it lies on whoever would lose if the trial stopped right then with no evidence. [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 105: On whom burden of proof lies

Q: How does this rule help judges manage complex trials with multiple defenses and counter-claims?
A: It gives them a simple, dynamic test to figure out which party currently has the legal obligation to produce the next piece of evidence to avoid losing the case. [Source: Section 105, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: On whom burden of proof lies

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: Who must prove a specific fact, like a defendant's alibi, to a judge?
A: The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on the person who wishes the Court to believe in its existence. [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: What rule does Section 106 of BSA 2023 establish regarding proving particular facts?
A: Section 106 of BSA 2023 establishes that the burden of proving a particular fact lies on the person wishing the Court to believe it exists, unless the law specifically places the burden elsewhere. [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: In a theft trial, A claims B confessed to a friend, while B claims he was out of town during the theft. Who proves what?
A: A must prove the admission happened, and B must prove his alibi of being out of town, as each wishes the Court to believe their respective facts. [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: What specific desire must a person have regarding a particular fact to trigger the burden of proof under this section?
A: The person must be the one 'who wishes the Court to believe in its existence.' [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: Is the person who wishes the Court to believe a fact always required to prove it without exception?
A: No, the section includes the exception 'unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person.' [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 106: Burden of proof as to particular fact

Q: How does this rule simplify the evidentiary process for isolated claims?
A: It prevents parties from throwing out unproven accusations or alibis and forcing the other side to disprove them, strictly tying the burden to the party asserting the specific fact. [Source: Section 106, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to particular fact

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: If a lawyer wants to introduce a dying declaration, who has to prove that the person who made it is actually dead?
A: The burden of proving the person's death is on the lawyer who wishes to give the dying declaration as evidence. [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: What does Section 107 of BSA 2023 say about the burden of proving foundational facts for evidence?
A: Section 107 of BSA 2023 says that the burden of proving any fact necessary to enable a person to give evidence of another fact is on the person wishing to give that evidence. [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: A party wants to submit a photocopy (secondary evidence) instead of an original contract. What must they prove first before the judge will look at the photocopy?
A: They must prove the foundational fact that the original document has been lost, because they are the person who wishes to give the secondary evidence. [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: What kind of relationship must exist between the two facts for this section to apply?
A: One fact must be 'necessary to be proved in order to enable any person to give evidence of any other fact.' [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: Can a judge waive the requirement for a party to prove the foundational fact if the secondary evidence looks very authentic?
A: No, the burden is strictly on the person wishing to give the evidence to prove the necessary enabling fact first. [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 107: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

Q: How does this rule protect against the premature introduction of inadmissible evidence?
A: It acts as a gatekeeper, forcing parties to legally establish the prerequisites (like a document being lost or a person being dead) before they can present the actual substantive evidence to the court. [Source: Section 107, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: If a defendant claims they committed an assault in self-defense, does the prosecutor have to prove it wasn't self-defense?
A: No, the burden of proving circumstances bringing the case within a General Exception like self-defense is upon the accused, and the Court shall presume the absence of such circumstances. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: What does Section 108 of BSA 2023 mandate when an accused relies on a legal exception?
A: Section 108 of BSA 2023 mandates that the accused has the burden of proving their case falls under any exception in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, while the Court presumes those circumstances are absent. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: A is charged with murder but claims insanity (unsoundness of mind) prevented him from knowing the nature of his act. Who must prove the insanity?
A: The burden of proof is on A, the accused, to prove the unsoundness of mind. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: Under what specific statute must the 'General Exceptions' or 'special exception or proviso' be contained for this rule to apply?
A: They must be contained in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or in any law defining the offence. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: Is there any situation under this section where the Court assumes the accused's claim of a General Exception might be true before they prove it?
A: No, the section explicitly states 'the Court shall presume the absence of such circumstances' until the accused proves otherwise. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 108: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

Q: What heavy evidentiary load does this section place on criminal defendants relying on affirmative defenses?
A: It forces defendants to actively prove their innocence through the defense (like provocation or insanity) rather than just poking holes in the prosecution's basic case. [Source: Section 108, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that case of accused comes within exceptions

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: If someone is caught on a train without showing a ticket, whose job is it to prove they actually bought one?
A: The burden of proving that he had a ticket is on the person travelling, because that fact is especially within his knowledge. [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: What is the core principle of Section 109 of BSA 2023 regarding burden of proof?
A: Section 109 of BSA 2023 states that when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him. [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: A person is found carrying a suspicious tool near a bank vault at night. They claim they were just walking home from a construction job. Who must prove this innocent intention?
A: The person must prove their intention, as they did an act with an intention other than what the circumstances suggest, placing the burden of proving that intention upon them. [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: What exact phrase describes the specific type of fact that shifts the burden of proof to a specific person under this section?
A: The fact must be 'especially within the knowledge' of that person. [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: Does this section apply to facts that are publicly documented and easily discoverable by both parties?
A: No, it strictly applies only to facts that are 'especially within the knowledge' of one specific person (like personal intent or possessing a small personal ticket). [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 109: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Q: How does this rule prevent the prosecution from facing impossible evidentiary burdens?
A: It prevents the prosecution from having to prove negative or deeply personal facts (like 'he didn't buy a ticket' or 'what he was secretly thinking') when the defendant holds all the proof. [Source: Section 109, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving fact especially within knowledge

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: If a man was seen alive 20 years ago, and someone now claims he is dead to claim his inheritance, who has to prove he died?
A: The burden of proving that he is dead is on the person who affirms it, because it is shown he was alive within thirty years. [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: What presumption of life does Section 110 of BSA 2023 establish?
A: Section 110 of BSA 2023 establishes that if a person was known to be alive within the last thirty years, the burden of proving their death falls on the person claiming they are dead. [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: A landlord wants to terminate a lease because the tenant allegedly died. The tenant's family proves the tenant paid rent in person 15 years ago. Who must prove the tenant is now dead?
A: The landlord must prove the tenant is dead, because the tenant was shown to be alive within thirty years. [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: What specific time frame of known life triggers the burden of proof to shift to the person claiming death?
A: The person must be shown to have been 'alive within thirty years.' [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: If it is shown a person was last alive 35 years ago, does this specific section put the burden on the person claiming death?
A: No, this section strictly applies when it is shown the person was alive 'within thirty years.' [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 110: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

Q: What legal stability does this 30-year presumption provide to long-term property and family arrangements?
A: It prevents opportunists from easily seizing property or dissolving marriages simply by alleging someone has died, forcing them to provide actual proof of death if the person was alive relatively recently. [Source: Section 110, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving death of person known to have been alive within thirty years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: If a woman has been missing and completely unheard from by her family for eight years, who has the burden of proving she is still alive?
A: The burden of proving she is alive is shifted to the person who affirms it, because she has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally hear of her. [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: How does Section 111 of BSA 2023 handle the presumption of death for missing persons?
A: Section 111 of BSA 2023 states that if a person has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally hear of them, the burden of proving they are alive shifts to whoever affirms it. [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: A wife wants to remarry because her husband disappeared on a voyage 10 years ago and no relatives have heard from him. If an insurance company claims he is secretly alive to avoid a payout, what must the company do?
A: The insurance company has the burden of proving that he is alive, because he has not been heard of for seven years. [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: What two conditions must be met regarding the missing person to shift the burden of proving life to the affirming party?
A: It must be proved that he has 'not been heard of for seven years' and this lack of hearing must be 'by those who would naturally have heard of him if he had been alive.' [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: If a fugitive intentionally cuts off all contact with their family for seven years while living next door to the police, does the family automatically get the benefit of this presumption?
A: Yes, because the text only requires that they have not been heard of for seven years by those who would 'naturally have heard of him,' shifting the burden to the police to prove he is alive. [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 111: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Q: By shifting the burden of proof, how does this 'civil death' rule help families of missing persons?
A: It allows families to legally move on, settle estates, and claim life insurance without facing the impossible task of proving the physical death of someone lost at sea or in a disaster. [Source: Section 111, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proving that person is alive who has not been heard of for seven years

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: If two people have been running a shop together as partners for years, and one suddenly claims they were never partners to avoid a business debt, who must prove it?
A: The burden of proving that they do not stand in that relationship is on the person who affirms it, since they have been shown to be acting as partners. [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: What presumption does Section 112 of BSA 2023 create regarding established business relationships?
A: Section 112 of BSA 2023 creates a presumption that if people have been acting as partners, landlord/tenant, or principal/agent, the burden of proving the relationship doesn't exist (or ceased) is on the one claiming so. [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: A tenant has paid rent to a landlord every month for five years. The tenant suddenly stops, claiming the landlord's lease expired. Who has the burden of proof?
A: The tenant has the burden of proving they have ceased to stand in the landlord and tenant relationship, as they are affirming the relationship ended. [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: What specific legal relationships are explicitly covered by the burden of proof rule in this section?
A: The relationships of 'partners,' 'landlord and tenant,' and 'principal and agent.' [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: Does this rule apply if two people are just friends who occasionally lend each other money?
A: No, the section strictly lists specific formal relationships (partners, landlord/tenant, principal/agent) where they have been 'acting as such.' [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 112: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

Q: How does this section maintain stability in commercial and property dealings?
A: It prevents parties from abruptly dodging their legal responsibilities by denying a long-standing, mutually acted-upon relationship, forcing them to produce hard evidence if they claim the relationship ended. [Source: Section 112, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to relationship in the cases of partners, landlord and tenant, principal and agent

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: If a person is physically holding and driving a car, and a stranger walks up and claims the car isn't theirs, who has to prove ownership?
A: The stranger must prove the driver is not the owner, because the burden of proving a person is not the owner is on the one affirming it when that person is shown to be in possession. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: How does Section 113 of BSA 2023 link possession to the burden of proof regarding ownership?
A: Section 113 of BSA 2023 states that when a person is shown to be in possession of anything, the burden of proving they are not the owner falls on the person asserting they are not. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: A is wearing a luxury watch. B sues A, claiming A stole the watch from B's house. Does A have to immediately produce a receipt to prove they own it?
A: No, because A is shown to be in possession of the watch, the burden of proving A is not the owner is on B. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: What specific physical or factual state must a person be shown to be in regarding the 'anything' to gain the protection of this presumption?
A: The person must be 'shown to be in possession' of it. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: If A simply points at a distant mountain and claims to own it, does the burden shift to others to disprove A's ownership?
A: No, the burden only shifts if A is actually 'shown to be in possession' of the item in question. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 113: Burden of proof as to ownership

Q: What fundamental legal concept regarding property rights does this section codify into evidentiary law?
A: It codifies the concept that 'possession is nine-tenths of the law,' giving a strong evidentiary advantage to the person actually holding or occupying the property. [Source: Section 113, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Burden of proof as to ownership
