Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: If an advocate buys a house from their own client for a very low price, and the client later sues claiming unfairness, who must prove the deal was fair?
A: The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the advocate, because they stand in a position of active confidence to the client. [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: What burden does Section 114 of BSA 2023 place on parties in a position of active confidence?
A: Section 114 of BSA 2023 places the burden of proving the good faith of a transaction on the party who stands in a position of active confidence to the other party. [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: An 18-year-old son sells his inherited estate to his father. The son later sues, claiming his father pressured him. Who has to prove the sale was conducted in good faith?
A: The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father, as he is in a position of active confidence over the son who just came of age. [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: What specific type of relationship must exist between the parties for the burden of proof to shift to the dominant party?
A: One party must stand to the other in a 'position of active confidence.' [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: Does this section reverse the burden of proof if a person buys a car from a completely unknown, random stranger?
A: No, it only applies when there is a question of good faith between parties where one is 'in relation of active confidence.' [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 114: Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence

Q: How does this rule protect vulnerable individuals in legal and familial relationships?
A: It protects them by presuming that professionals or authoritative family members might use their influence unfairly, forcing the dominant party to actively prove they didn't exploit the trust placed in them. [Source: Section 114, BSA 2023]

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: If a person is found in an officially declared disturbed area while an armed mob is shooting at police from that exact spot, what does the law presume?
A: The law presumes, unless the contrary is shown, that the person committed the specified offences (like rioting or criminal conspiracy) against the armed forces or police. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: What presumption does Section 115 of BSA 2023 authorize regarding areas with extensive public disturbance?
A: Section 115 of BSA 2023 authorizes a presumption that a person present in a disturbed area where armed attacks on forces occurred committed specific rioting or conspiracy offences, unless they prove otherwise. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: A is arrested in a location where a mob used explosives against public order forces. The area had experienced extensive peace disturbance for two months. What burden does A face?
A: A faces the burden of showing they did not commit an offence like rioting, because the Court shall presume they did commit it due to their presence during the attack in a disturbed area. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: What two specific types of weapons must be used against the armed forces from that place to trigger this presumption?
A: 'Firearms or explosives' must be used. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: Does this presumption apply if a person is present during a peaceful protest in a normal area where no firearms are used?
A: No, the presumption strictly requires the area to be a declared 'disturbed area' or have extensive disturbance for over a month, and firearms or explosives must be used to attack forces from that place. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 115: Presumption as to certain offences

Q: How does this severe presumption aid law enforcement during violent riots or insurgencies?
A: It relieves the prosecution of the difficult task of proving the specific individual actions of every rioter in a chaotic armed mob, shifting the burden to those present to prove their innocence. [Source: Section 115, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to certain offences

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: Does the law automatically assume a child born to a married woman is the legitimate child of her husband?
A: Yes, the fact that a person was born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man shall be conclusive proof that he is the legitimate child of that man. [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: What presumption does Section 116 of BSA 2023 establish regarding a child born within 280 days after a marriage dissolves?
A: Section 116 of BSA 2023 establishes that a child born within two hundred and eighty days after the dissolution of a valid marriage, the mother remaining unmarried, is conclusively proved to be the legitimate child of that man. [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: A child is born to a married couple. The husband suspects the child is not his and wants to do a DNA test just because of his suspicion. How does the court view the child's legitimacy based solely on the marriage?
A: The Court views the birth during the valid marriage as conclusive proof of legitimacy, unless the husband can show he had no access to the mother when the child could have been begotten. [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: What specific time limit applies to the presumption of legitimacy if the child is born after the dissolution of the marriage?
A: The child must be born 'within two hundred and eighty days after its dissolution.' [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: Is there any way for a husband to overcome this 'conclusive proof' of legitimacy for a child born during the marriage?
A: Yes, the conclusive proof can be overcome 'unless it can be shown that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten.' [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 116: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Q: By making this proof 'conclusive,' what invasive public inquiries does the law generally prevent?
A: It prevents invasive inquiries and disputes into the paternity of children born within valid marriages, protecting the child's status unless strict non-access is proven. [Source: Section 116, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: If a woman commits suicide within seven years of her marriage after being subjected to cruelty by her husband, what can the court presume?
A: The Court may presume, having regard to all other circumstances, that such suicide had been abetted by her husband or the relative who subjected her to cruelty. [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: What discretionary presumption does Section 117 of BSA 2023 authorize regarding a married woman's suicide?
A: Section 117 of BSA 2023 authorizes the Court to presume that a husband or his relative abetted the woman's suicide if she died within seven years of marriage and had been subjected to cruelty by them. [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: A woman tragicially ends her own life 10 years after her wedding. Her parents prove her husband's family was cruel to her. Does the presumption under this specific section apply?
A: No, because the section strictly requires that the suicide must have been committed 'within a period of seven years from the date of her marriage.' [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: What specific statutory definition must be used to interpret the word 'cruelty' in this section?
A: 'Cruelty' shall have the same meaning as in section 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: Is the court forced to automatically declare the husband guilty of abetment if the suicide happens within seven years and cruelty is shown?
A: No, the Court 'may presume' it, meaning it is a discretionary presumption, and the Court must do so 'having regard to all the other circumstances of the case.' [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 117: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

Q: How does this presumption assist in prosecuting domestic abuse that leads to suicide?
A: It bridges the evidentiary gap between the cruelty and the secret act of suicide, allowing the court to link the abuse to the death without needing direct evidence of someone explicitly telling the victim to die. [Source: Section 117, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to abetment of suicide by a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: If a woman is killed soon after her husband harassed her for dowry, does the prosecutor have to prove he directly caused the death?
A: When it is shown she was subjected to cruelty or harassment in connection with a dowry demand soon before her death, the Court shall presume that the person caused the dowry death. [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: What mandatory presumption does Section 118 of BSA 2023 establish regarding dowry deaths?
A: Section 118 of BSA 2023 establishes a mandatory presumption that a person caused a dowry death if they subjected the woman to cruelty or harassment for dowry soon before her death. [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: A woman dies under suspicious circumstances. Her family proves her husband harassed her for a car (dowry) just a week before she died. How does the court proceed?
A: The Court shall presume that the husband caused the dowry death, placing the burden on him to prove his innocence. [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: What specific legal cross-reference defines the term 'dowry death' for the purposes of this evidentiary section?
A: The Explanation states 'dowry death' shall have the same meaning as in section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: If a husband harassed his wife for dowry five years ago, but completely stopped, and she dies suddenly now, does this presumption immediately apply?
A: No, the section requires it to be shown that the cruelty or harassment occurred 'soon before her death.' [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 118: Presumption as to dowry death

Q: Why does the law use the phrase 'shall presume' here instead of 'may presume' as in the previous suicide section?
A: It reflects a strict legislative intent to deal harshly with dowry deaths, forcing courts to automatically shift the burden of proof to the accused once the pre-death harassment is established. [Source: Section 118, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: Can a judge use common sense to assume an official document was processed normally if there is no evidence suggesting otherwise?
A: Yes, the Court may presume the existence of any fact it thinks likely to have happened, including that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed. [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: What general power does Section 119 of BSA 2023 give to the Court regarding likely facts?
A: Section 119 of BSA 2023 gives the Court the discretionary power to presume the existence of facts likely to have happened based on the common course of natural events, human conduct, and business. [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: A man is caught walking out of an electronics store holding a laptop that was stolen 10 minutes ago. He has no receipt. What can the court presume under Illustration (a)?
A: The Court may presume that the man is either the thief or received the goods knowing them to be stolen, unless he can account for his possession. [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: According to Illustration (g), what may the Court presume about evidence that a person could produce but chooses to withhold?
A: The Court may presume that the evidence, if produced, 'would be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.' [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: If a man possesses a stolen marked rupee, but he is a shopkeeper constantly receiving coins, does the court have to presume he is a thief?
A: No, sub-section (2)(i) states the Court shall have regard to those circumstances, meaning it can choose not to apply the presumption of theft to the shopkeeper. [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 119: Court may presume existence of certain facts

Q: How does this section allow courts to function practically without requiring absolute proof for every minor detail?
A: It allows courts to rely on established patterns of human and institutional behavior (like letters arriving in the mail or accomplices being untrustworthy) to fill minor evidentiary gaps logically. [Source: Section 119, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court may presume existence of certain facts

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: In a rape trial where sexual intercourse is proven, and the victim testifies she did not consent, must the prosecutor find additional witnesses to prove she said no?
A: No, if she states in her evidence before the Court that she did not consent, the Court shall presume that she did not consent. [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: What mandatory presumption does Section 120 of BSA 2023 create in specific rape prosecutions?
A: Section 120 of BSA 2023 mandates that if sexual intercourse is proved and the woman testifies she did not consent, the Court shall presume she did not consent. [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: During a trial under section 64(2) of the BNS, the medical evidence proves sexual intercourse occurred. The woman takes the stand and swears she did not agree to it. How does the judge weigh her statement regarding consent?
A: The judge is legally bound to presume that she did not consent, based solely on her statement in evidence before the Court. [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: Under what specific section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 must the prosecution be taking place for this presumption to apply?
A: The prosecution must be for rape under 'sub-section (2) of section 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.' [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: Does this section apply if the prosecution fails to actually prove that sexual intercourse took place at all?
A: No, the presumption only triggers 'where sexual intercourse by the accused is proved.' [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 120: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

Q: How does this presumption protect the dignity and testimony of victims in rape trials?
A: It prevents the defense from arguing that a lack of physical resistance implies consent, elevating the woman's direct courtroom testimony of non-consent to a legal presumption the accused must overcome. [Source: Section 120, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Presumption as to absence of consent in certain prosecution for rape

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: If a person intentionally tricks someone into believing a lie, can they later admit it was a lie to win a lawsuit against that person?
A: No, when a person intentionally causes another to believe a thing and act upon it, they are not allowed to deny the truth of that thing in a suit against that person. [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: What legal principle does Section 121 of BSA 2023 establish regarding intentional misrepresentations?
A: Section 121 of BSA 2023 establishes the principle of estoppel, preventing a person from denying the truth of something they previously, intentionally caused another person to believe and act upon. [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: A falsely convinces B that A owns a farm, prompting B to buy it. Later, A actually inherits the farm and tries to cancel the sale because they didn't legally own it when they sold it. Can A do this?
A: No, A must not be allowed to prove his want of title, because he is estopped by his previous intentional and false declaration to B. [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: Through what three specific modes of conduct can a person intentionally cause another to believe a thing to be true under this section?
A: Through his 'declaration, act or omission.' [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: Does the rule of estoppel apply if the person accidentally misspoke, without any intention of causing the other person to believe the thing?
A: No, the section strictly requires that the person has 'intentionally caused' the other person to believe the thing to be true. [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 121: Estoppel

Q: How does the doctrine of estoppel protect the integrity of commercial and personal dealings?
A: It forces people to stand by their representations and prevents them from profiting off their own deceit by changing their story after someone else has acted on it. [Source: Section 121, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: While renting an apartment, can a tenant refuse to pay rent by suddenly claiming the landlord doesn't actually own the building?
A: No, no tenant shall be permitted to deny that the landlord had a title to the immovable property at the beginning of the tenancy. [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: What specific type of estoppel does Section 122 of BSA 2023 apply to property relationships?
A: Section 122 of BSA 2023 applies estoppel to tenants and licensees, preventing them from denying the title of the landlord or the licensor who gave them possession. [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: A allows B to park their car on A's driveway (a licence). B later gets towed by A and sues, claiming A never owned the driveway anyway. Can B make this claim?
A: No, as a licensee, B shall not be permitted to deny that A (the person in possession) had a title to such possession at the time the licence was given. [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: During what specific timeframes is a tenant barred from denying the landlord's title under this section?
A: The tenant is barred 'during the continuance of the tenancy or any time thereafter.' [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: Does this section prevent a tenant from proving that the landlord *lost* their title to the property five years *after* the tenancy began?
A: No, the estoppel specifically prevents the tenant from denying that the landlord had a title 'at the beginning of the tenancy.' [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 122: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

Q: By enforcing this rule, what chaotic legal situation between property owners and occupants is avoided?
A: It avoids a situation where occupants enjoy the benefits of a lease or license but then turn around and legally harass the owner by challenging the very property rights they initially accepted. [Source: Section 122, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of tenant and of licensee of person in possession

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: If a bank accepts a bill of exchange, can it later refuse to pay by claiming the person who drew it had no authority to do so?
A: No, no acceptor of a bill of exchange shall be permitted to deny that the drawer had authority to draw such bill or to endorse it. [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: How does Section 123 of BSA 2023 restrict the defenses available to bailees?
A: Section 123 of BSA 2023 estops bailees from denying that their bailor had the authority to make the bailment at the time it commenced. [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: A stores furniture with a warehouse (bailee). The warehouse gives the furniture to B, claiming B is the true owner. If A sues the warehouse, can the warehouse defend itself by saying A never had authority to store it?
A: Yes, according to Explanation 2, if a bailee delivers the goods to a person other than the bailor, he may prove that such person had a right to them as against the bailor. [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: What specific action can the acceptor of a bill of exchange still deny, according to Explanation 1, despite the general estoppel?
A: The acceptor may deny that the bill was 'really drawn by the person by whom it purports to have been drawn' (i.e., they can allege forgery). [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: Is a licensee completely barred from questioning the licensor's authority forever?
A: They are only estopped from denying the licensor had authority 'at the time when the... licence commenced.' [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 123: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

Q: What specific commercial trust does this estoppel rule facilitate in the banking and warehousing sectors?
A: It facilitates trust in negotiable instruments and storage contracts by preventing the accepting institutions from undermining the fundamental authority of the person they initially chose to do business with. [Source: Section 123, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Estoppel of acceptor of bill of exchange, bailee or licensee

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: Can an extremely old person or a young child serve as a witness in a court case?
A: Yes, all persons shall be competent to testify unless the Court considers they are prevented from understanding the questions or giving rational answers due to tender years, old age, or disease. [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: What broad rule regarding witness competency does Section 124 of BSA 2023 establish?
A: Section 124 of BSA 2023 establishes that all persons are competent to testify, provided they can understand questions and give rational answers, regardless of age or physical/mental disease. [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: A person with a diagnosed mental illness witnesses a crime. The defense argues they cannot testify. What specific test must the judge apply to decide?
A: The judge must determine if the person's unsoundness of mind prevents them from understanding the questions put to them and giving rational answers. [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: Name three specific causes listed in the section that might prompt a court to evaluate if a person is prevented from giving rational answers.
A: The section lists 'tender years,' 'extreme old age,' and 'disease, whether of body or mind.' [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: Is a person of unsound mind automatically and permanently incompetent to testify?
A: No, the Explanation states a person of unsound mind is not incompetent unless their condition specifically prevents them from understanding questions and giving rational answers. [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 124: Who may testify

Q: By focusing on cognitive ability rather than medical labels, how does this section maximize the court's access to evidence?
A: It prevents the automatic exclusion of children, the elderly, or the mentally ill, allowing the court to hear vital testimony as long as the witness is practically capable of communicating facts reliably. [Source: Section 124, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Who may testify

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: If a witness is unable to speak, can they write their answers down or use sign language in court?
A: Yes, a witness who is unable to speak may give evidence in any intelligible manner, such as by writing or signs, provided it is done in open Court. [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: How does Section 125 of BSA 2023 classify evidence given through writing or signs by a non-verbal witness?
A: Section 125 of BSA 2023 mandates that evidence given by a non-verbal witness through writing or signs in open Court shall be legally deemed to be 'oral evidence.' [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: A deaf and mute witness testifies using sign language. To ensure accuracy, what two specific procedural safeguards must the Court implement according to the proviso?
A: The Court must take the assistance of an interpreter or a special educator in recording the statement, and the statement must be videographed. [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: Where exactly must the writing be written or the signs made for this type of evidence to be valid?
A: They must be written or made 'in open Court.' [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: Does this section apply to a witness who *can* speak but simply refuses to do so out of stubbornness?
A: No, the section explicitly applies to 'A witness who is unable to speak' or 'unable to communicate verbally.' [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 125: Witness unable to communicate verbally

Q: By deeming this non-verbal communication as 'oral evidence,' what legal categorization issue is resolved?
A: It ensures that written notes or signs made live in court are treated with the same immediate evidentiary weight and cross-examination rules as spoken testimony, rather than being treated as 'documentary evidence.' [Source: Section 125, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness unable to communicate verbally

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: In a civil lawsuit, can a wife be called to testify as a witness in her husband's case?
A: Yes, in all civil proceedings, the husband or wife of any party to the suit shall be a competent witness. [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: What rule does Section 126 of BSA 2023 establish regarding spousal testimony in criminal cases?
A: Section 126 of BSA 2023 establishes that in criminal proceedings against any person, the husband or wife of such person shall be a competent witness. [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: A man is on trial for a robbery. The prosecutor wants to call the man's wife to the stand to testify about his whereabouts. Can the defense argue she is legally incompetent to testify just because she is his wife?
A: No, the defense cannot argue that, because in criminal proceedings against any person, the wife of such person shall be a competent witness. [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: Does this section distinguish the competency of spouses based on whether the proceeding is civil or criminal?
A: No, it explicitly affirms that spouses are competent witnesses in both 'civil proceedings' and 'criminal proceedings.' [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: Are there any specific crimes listed in this section where a spouse is suddenly deemed incompetent to testify?
A: No, the section states broadly that in criminal proceedings against 'any person,' the spouse shall be a competent witness without listing exceptions. [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 126: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

Q: By removing the old common-law bar against spousal testimony, how does this rule aid modern fact-finding?
A: It ensures that courts have access to testimony from the people most likely to have intimate knowledge of a party's actions and whereabouts, treating spouses as competent witnesses like anyone else. [Source: Section 126, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Competency of husband and wife as witnesses in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: Can a lawyer force the judge from their previous trial to take the witness stand and explain why they made a specific ruling?
A: No, a Judge or Magistrate shall not be compelled to answer any question as to his own conduct in Court as such Judge, except upon the special order of a subordinate Court. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: What protection does Section 127 of BSA 2023 provide to judicial officers regarding their official duties?
A: Section 127 of BSA 2023 protects Judges and Magistrates from being compelled to answer questions about their conduct in Court or things that came to their knowledge as a Judge, unless ordered by a superior Court. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: During a murder trial before a Sessions Judge, the defendant suddenly pulls out a knife and tries to stab a police officer. Can the Sessions Judge later be called as a witness to describe the attack?
A: Yes, the Judge may be examined as to other matters which occurred in his presence whilst he was acting as a Judge, such as witnessing an attempted murder. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: What specific type of legal document is required to compel a Magistrate to testify about how they improperly took a deposition?
A: A 'special order of some Court to which he is subordinate' (a superior Court) is required. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: Is a judge completely immune from testifying about *anything* that happens in their courtroom?
A: No, the section explicitly states 'he may be examined as to other matters which occurred in his presence whilst he was so acting,' like witnessing a separate crime. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 127: Judges and Magistrates

Q: How does this privilege protect the independence and finality of the judicial process?
A: It prevents losing parties from endlessly harassing judges by dragging them into subsequent trials to justify their rulings or repeat confidential courtroom knowledge. [Source: Section 127, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judges and Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: If a husband privately confesses a crime to his wife, can the police later force the wife to tell the court what he said?
A: No, no person who is or has been married shall be compelled to disclose any communication made to them during marriage by their spouse. [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: How does Section 128 of BSA 2023 treat private conversations between married couples?
A: Section 128 of BSA 2023 treats communications during marriage as highly privileged, stating no person shall be compelled or permitted to disclose them without consent, with limited exceptions. [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: A wife wants to voluntarily testify against her husband about a secret he told her during their marriage, but the husband objects. Can she disclose the secret?
A: No, she shall not be permitted to disclose such communication unless the person who made it (the husband) consents. [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: What specific relationship status must the parties hold when the communication is made for this privilege to attach?
A: The communication must be made 'during marriage by any person to whom he is or has been married.' [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: In what two specific types of legal actions does this marital communication privilege completely disappear?
A: It disappears in 'suits between married persons, or proceedings in which one married person is prosecuted for any crime committed against the other.' [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 128: Communications during marriage

Q: What fundamental social institution is this rule designed to protect by ensuring absolute confidentiality?
A: It is designed to protect the institution of marriage, ensuring spouses can communicate with complete trust and candor without fear that their private words will be weaponized in court. [Source: Section 128, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Communications during marriage

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: Can a citizen demand that unpublished, highly classified government documents be presented as evidence in their civil lawsuit?
A: No, no one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State without permission. [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: Who holds the power under Section 129 of BSA 2023 to allow evidence regarding affairs of State to be presented?
A: Section 129 of BSA 2023 places the power solely with the officer at the head of the department concerned, who shall give or withhold permission as he thinks fit. [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: A whistleblower tries to submit a stolen, unpublished defense ministry memo in a corruption trial. The head of the defense ministry refuses to allow it. Can the judge overrule the ministry head and accept the memo?
A: No, the evidence cannot be permitted except with the permission of the head of the department concerned, who has absolute discretion to withhold it. [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: What specific type of official records does this absolute privilege against disclosure apply to?
A: It applies strictly to 'unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State.' [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: Does this section provide a mechanism for a judge to review the unpublished records privately to decide if they should be released anyway?
A: No, the section grants the power to give or withhold permission entirely to the 'officer at the head of the department concerned,' not the court. [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 129: Evidence as to affairs of State

Q: How does this strict rule prioritize national security over individual legal disputes?
A: It ensures that sensitive government secrets, diplomatic correspondence, and defense strategies cannot be forcibly exposed through standard courtroom evidence procedures, protecting the broader interests of the State. [Source: Section 129, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence as to affairs of State

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: If a citizen sends a confidential tip to a police inspector, can the defense lawyer force the inspector to reveal what the tip said in court?
A: No, no public officer shall be compelled to disclose communications made to him in official confidence, when he considers that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure. [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: What discretion does Section 130 of BSA 2023 grant to public officers regarding confidential information?
A: Section 130 of BSA 2023 grants public officers the discretion to refuse to disclose communications made to them in official confidence if they believe disclosure would harm public interests. [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: A tax officer receives a secret dossier about a company's finances from an anonymous source. During a related lawsuit, the company demands to see the dossier. Who decides if it must be shown?
A: The public officer (the tax officer) decides; they cannot be compelled to disclose it if they consider that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure. [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: In what specific context must the communication be made to the public officer for this privilege to apply?
A: It must be a communication made to him 'in official confidence.' [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: If a public officer believes releasing a confidential letter won't harm the public interest, but will embarrass a politician, can they use this section to hide it?
A: The section specifically limits the privilege to situations 'when he considers that the public interests would suffer by the disclosure,' not personal or political embarrassment. [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 130: Official communications

Q: Why is it important for the law to protect these 'official confidence' communications?
A: It ensures that citizens, informants, and junior officials can safely report sensitive information to authorities without fear of public exposure, maintaining the free flow of intelligence to the government. [Source: Section 130, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Official communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: Can a defense lawyer force a police officer on the stand to reveal the name of the confidential informant who gave them the initial tip?
A: No, no police officer shall be compelled to say when he got any information as to the commission of any offence. [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: What specific protection does Section 131 of BSA 2023 provide to revenue officers?
A: Section 131 of BSA 2023 provides that no revenue officer shall be compelled to say when he got any information as to the commission of any offence against the public revenue. [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: A tax inspector (revenue officer) receives an anonymous tip about a massive corporate tax evasion scheme. In court, the corporation demands to know exactly what time and day the tip was received. Must the officer answer?
A: No, the revenue officer cannot be compelled to say when he got any information as to the commission of the offence against public revenue. [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: How does the Explanation define a 'revenue officer' for the purposes of this section?
A: It defines a 'revenue officer' as 'any officer employed in or about the business of any branch of the public revenue.' [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: Is there any exception listed in this section that allows a judge to force a magistrate to reveal when they received information if it is crucial to the defense?
A: No, the section states unconditionally that 'No Magistrate or police officer shall be compelled to say' without listing any exceptions. [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 131: Information as to commission of offences

Q: How does this rule protect the intelligence-gathering capabilities of law enforcement?
A: It protects law enforcement by allowing officers to keep the specific timing (and impliedly the sources) of their confidential tips secret, encouraging informants to come forward without fear of exposure in court. [Source: Section 131, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to commission of offences

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: If a client privately admits to their lawyer that they committed a past murder, can the lawyer tell the police?
A: No, an advocate shall not be permitted to disclose any communication made to him by his client in the course of his service, unless with the client's express consent. [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: How does Section 132 of BSA 2023 protect the confidentiality of legal documents?
A: Section 132 of BSA 2023 prohibits an advocate from stating the contents or condition of any document they became acquainted with in the course and for the purpose of their professional service. [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: A client hires an advocate and says, 'I plan to use this forged deed to steal my neighbor's land; please file the lawsuit.' Is this communication protected by attorney-client privilege?
A: No, this communication is not protected because it is made in furtherance of a criminal purpose (obtaining property by a forged deed). [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: According to sub-section (3), to what other legal staff do the strict confidentiality rules of this section apply?
A: The provisions shall apply to 'interpreters, and the clerks or employees of advocates.' [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: If an advocate notices a forged entry added to a client's account book *after* the lawyer was hired, is that observation protected?
A: No, the proviso exempts any fact observed by an advocate showing that a crime or fraud has been committed 'since the commencement of his service.' [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 132: Professional communications

Q: Why is the lawyer-client privilege stated in this section essential to the justice system?
A: It ensures clients can be completely honest with their advocates without fear of betrayal, which is necessary for the advocate to provide a proper legal defense. [Source: Section 132, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Professional communications

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: If a party simply takes the witness stand to testify in their own case, does that automatically mean their lawyer is now free to reveal all their secret conversations?
A: No, if a party gives evidence at his own instance, he shall not be deemed to have consented thereby to such disclosure as is mentioned in section 132. [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: What does Section 133 of BSA 2023 clarify about calling an advocate as a witness?
A: Section 133 of BSA 2023 clarifies that calling one's advocate as a witness only waives privilege if the party specifically questions the advocate on matters the advocate would otherwise not be at liberty to disclose. [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: A client testifies in court. Later, the opposing lawyer argues that by testifying, the client waived attorney-client privilege and demands to cross-examine the client's lawyer. Is the opposing lawyer correct?
A: No, merely giving evidence does not mean the party is deemed to have consented to the disclosure of protected professional communications. [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: Under what specific condition is a party deemed to have consented to disclosure if they call their own advocate to the stand?
A: They are deemed to have consented 'only if he questions such advocate, on matters which, but for such question, he would not be at liberty to disclose.' [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: Is there any situation under this section where volunteering general evidence accidentally waives the section 132 privilege?
A: No, the section explicitly prevents accidental waiver, stating the party 'shall not be deemed to have consented thereby' just by volunteering evidence. [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 133: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

Q: How does this section protect a client's right to testify in their own defense?
A: It allows clients to freely take the stand to defend themselves without the terrifying risk that doing so will automatically strip away their attorney-client privilege and expose all their private legal consultations. [Source: Section 133, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Privilege not waived by volunteering evidence

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: Can a prosecutor force a defendant to reveal what they privately discussed with their lawyer before the trial?
A: No, no one shall be compelled to disclose to the Court any confidential communication which has taken place between him and his legal adviser. [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: What protection does Section 134 of BSA 2023 offer directly to the client regarding legal advice?
A: Section 134 of BSA 2023 protects the client from being compelled to disclose to the Court any confidential communication between them and their legal adviser. [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: A client volunteers to be a witness and gives testimony that seems to contradict their initial legal filings. Can the court now compel them to reveal what they told their lawyer?
A: Yes, because they offered themselves as a witness, the Court may compel them to disclose such communications, but only those necessary to explain the evidence they just gave. [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: What specific action by the client triggers the exception allowing the Court to compel disclosure of these communications?
A: The exception is triggered 'unless he offers himself as a witness.' [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: If a client testifies, can the court force them to reveal *every* single conversation they ever had with their lawyer?
A: No, the court may only compel disclosure of such communications 'as may appear to the Court necessary to be known in order to explain any evidence which he has given, but no others.' [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 134: Confidential communication with legal advisers

Q: How does this section complement Section 132 (Professional communications)?
A: While Section 132 gags the *advocate* from revealing secrets, Section 134 protects the *client* from being forced to reveal those same secrets, ensuring the privilege cannot be bypassed by simply interrogating the client instead. [Source: Section 134, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Confidential communication with legal advisers

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: If a random person is called as a witness in someone else's property dispute, can the court force them to bring in the private title deeds to their own house?
A: No, a witness who is not a party to a suit shall not be compelled to produce his title-deeds to any property. [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: What protection does Section 135 of BSA 2023 give to third-party witnesses regarding their property documents?
A: Section 135 of BSA 2023 protects a witness who is not a party from being compelled to produce their title-deeds, pledge/mortgage documents, or any document that might criminate them. [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: A bank holds a property deed as a mortgagee. The bank is subpoenaed as a third-party witness in a lawsuit entirely unrelated to them. Can the bank be forced to produce the deed?
A: No, a witness not a party cannot be compelled to produce any document in virtue of which they hold property as a mortgagee, unless they agreed in writing to do so. [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: Aside from title-deeds and mortgage documents, what other specific type of document is protected from compelled production under this section?
A: 'Any document the production of which might tend to criminate him.' [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: Under what specific, documented condition *can* a non-party witness be compelled to produce their title deeds?
A: They can be compelled 'unless he has agreed in writing to produce them with the person seeking the production of such deeds or some person through whom he claims.' [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 135: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

Q: Why does the law shield third-party witnesses from handing over their private property deeds?
A: It protects innocent bystanders from having their own private property rights, titles, and potential liabilities needlessly exposed or endangered just because they were called to testify in someone else's legal battle. [Source: Section 135, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of title-deeds of witness not a party

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: Can a lawyer force a secretary to hand over confidential files if the boss who owns those files would have the right to refuse?
A: No, no one shall be compelled to produce documents in their possession if another person would be entitled to refuse to produce them if they had them. [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: What protection does Section 136 of BSA 2023 extend to agents holding documents for someone else?
A: Section 136 of BSA 2023 protects a person from being compelled to produce documents or electronic records under their control if the true owner would have a legal right to refuse production. [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: A client gives their highly privileged legal files to a courier for transport. The opposing lawyer subpoenas the courier to hand them over. Must the courier comply?
A: No, the courier cannot be compelled to produce them because the client (the other person) would be entitled to refuse production based on legal privilege. [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: What specific modern form of data storage is explicitly protected under this section alongside physical documents?
A: The section explicitly protects 'electronic records under his control.' [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: Under what single condition *can* the person holding the documents be forced to produce them despite the owner's underlying privilege?
A: They can be produced only if 'such last-mentioned person [the person with the right to refuse] consents to their production.' [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 136: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

Q: How does this rule prevent legal privileges from being bypassed through technicalities?
A: It prevents lawyers from exploiting the temporary physical transfer of sensitive documents (like giving them to a clerk or cloud provider) to break a privilege that rightfully belongs to the owner. [Source: Section 136, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Production of documents or electronic records which another person, having possession, could refuse to produce

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: Can a witness refuse to answer a relevant question in court simply by claiming the answer might get them arrested?
A: No, a witness shall not be excused from answering any relevant question upon the ground that the answer will criminate them. [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: What does Section 137 of BSA 2023 state about a witness's right against self-incrimination on the witness stand?
A: Section 137 of BSA 2023 states that a witness cannot refuse to answer a relevant question just because the answer might directly or indirectly criminate them or expose them to a penalty. [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: During a civil fraud trial, a witness is asked a relevant question about their involvement. They try to stay silent, arguing the answer proves they committed a crime. How must the court rule?
A: The court must compel them to answer, as they are not excused from answering relevant questions even if it exposes them to a penalty. [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: What essential characteristic must the question possess for the court to compel an answer despite the risk of self-incrimination?
A: The question must be 'as to any matter relevant to the matter in issue' in the proceeding. [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: Does this harsh rule mean the police can immediately use the witness's forced confession to throw them in jail?
A: No, the proviso guarantees that 'no such answer, which a witness shall be compelled to give, shall subject him to any arrest or prosecution, or be proved against him in any criminal proceeding.' [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 137: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

Q: What specific, secondary crime is the only one a witness *can* be prosecuted for based on their compelled testimony?
A: The only exception is a prosecution 'forgiving false evidence by such answer' (perjury). [Source: Section 137, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness not excused from answering on ground that answer will criminate

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: Can a person who helped commit a crime (an accomplice) testify in court against the main perpetrator?
A: Yes, an accomplice shall be a competent witness against an accused person. [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: How does Section 138 of BSA 2023 view the evidentiary value of an accomplice's testimony?
A: Section 138 of BSA 2023 establishes that an accomplice is a competent witness and that a conviction based upon the corroborated testimony of an accomplice is not illegal. [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: The getaway driver in a bank robbery testifies against the bank robber. The robber's lawyer argues the conviction must be thrown out because the only witness is a fellow criminal. Is this argument legally sound?
A: No, the argument is not sound because an accomplice is a competent witness, and the conviction is legal if it proceeds upon their corroborated testimony. [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: What specific adjective describes the type of testimony from an accomplice that makes a conviction legally secure under this section?
A: The testimony must be 'corroborated.' [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: Does this section say an uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice is strictly illegal?
A: The section specifically says a conviction is not illegal if it proceeds upon the 'corroborated testimony,' reflecting the general judicial caution required when dealing with accomplices. [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 138: Accomplice

Q: How does allowing accomplice testimony practically benefit criminal justice?
A: It allows prosecutors to break criminal conspiracies by offering leniency to minor participants in exchange for crucial insider testimony against the main offenders. [Source: Section 138, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accomplice

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: Does the law require a minimum of two eyewitnesses to prove that a murder happened?
A: No, no particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required for the proof of any fact. [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: What fundamental evidentiary principle does Section 139 of BSA 2023 lay down regarding the quantity of testimony?
A: Section 139 of BSA 2023 lays down the principle that the law does not require any specific number of witnesses to prove any fact. [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: A victim of an assault is the only person who saw the attacker. The defense argues the case must be dismissed because there are no other corroborating eyewitnesses. Will this argument succeed?
A: No, the argument will fail because no particular number of witnesses is required for proof; the single testimony of the victim can be sufficient if deemed credible. [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: Does this rule apply differently to serious crimes versus minor civil disputes?
A: No, the section explicitly states this applies 'in any case' for the proof of 'any fact.' [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: Are there any specific types of facts listed in this section that *do* require multiple witnesses?
A: No, the section contains no exceptions, stating 'No particular number... shall in any case be required'. [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 139: Number of witnesses

Q: How does this rule shift the focus of judicial evaluation during a trial?
A: It shifts the court's focus entirely away from counting the quantity of witnesses (a mechanical test) and toward evaluating the pure quality and credibility of the testimony given. [Source: Section 139, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Number of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: Who decides which witness gets called to the stand first during a trial?
A: The order shall be regulated by the law and practice relating to civil and criminal procedure, and in the absence of such law, by the discretion of the Court. [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: How does Section 140 of BSA 2023 direct courts to handle the order of examining witnesses?
A: Section 140 of BSA 2023 directs that the order of witness examination is governed by civil and criminal procedure laws, and falls to the Court's discretion if those laws are silent. [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: During a complex civil trial, neither the BSA nor the Civil Procedure Code gives a clear rule on whether expert witnesses must testify before lay witnesses. Who resolves this?
A: In the absence of any such law, the order shall be regulated by the discretion of the Court. [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: What two specific bodies of procedural law are referenced as the primary authority for regulating the order of witnesses?
A: 'The law and practice for the time being relating to civil and criminal procedure respectively.' [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: Can a judge arbitrarily decide the order of witnesses if there is already a clear statutory procedure laid out in the criminal procedure code?
A: No, the judge's discretion only applies 'in the absence of any such law.' [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 140: Order of production and examination of witnesses

Q: Why does the Evidence Act defer this logistical issue to procedural laws instead of creating strict rules itself?
A: The Evidence Act focuses on what is admissible, while procedural codes (like BNSS) are better equipped to handle the practical mechanics and flow of conducting a trial. [Source: Section 140, BSA 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order of production and examination of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - Section 141: Judge to decide as to admissibility of evidence

Q: When a lawyer tries to present a piece of evidence, who ultimately decides if it can be admitted in court?
